title: Bodhicaryāvatāra

atts.t:
Just as on a dark night, within the womb of clouds,
A flash of lightning shows brilliant illumination for an instant,
Likewise, by the power of the Buddha, occasionally
Intelligence for merit arises for a moment in the world.

i.sp: within the womb of clouds
i.ev: Tibetan སྤྲིན་རུམ་ན (Skt meghaghanāndhakāre) means 'in the thick mass of clouds'; bo-kunpal 1-5 glosses it as སྤྲིན་རུམ་ 'cloud-bank'. Nothing in the Tibetan or commentaries supports 'womb'.
i.fx: within a dense mass of clouds

i.sp: occasionally / Intelligence for merit arises for a moment in the world
i.ev: བརྒྱ་ལམ་ན 'once in a hundred (instances/paths)' and ཐང་འགའ་འབྱུང 'only rarely arises'; bo-shenga 1-5 ཐང་འགའ་ཙམ་འབྱུང་ངོ and bo-kunpal 1-5 (བརྒྱ་ལན་རེ་སྟོང་ལན་གཉིས་ཙམ་འབྱུང 'occurs about once in a hundred or thousand times'). 'For a moment' belongs to the lightning simile (སྐད་ཅིག), not to the arising of the thought (Skt kṣaṇaṃ is not in the Tibetan line); rarity is lost.
i.fx: once in a hundred times, the thought toward merit rarely arises in the world

atts.t:
Just as on a dark night, within a dense mass of clouds,
A flash of lightning shows brilliant illumination for an instant,
Likewise, by the power of the Buddha, once in a hundred times,
Intelligence for merit rarely arises in the world.

Since the sole caravan leader of wandering beings, with limitless intellect,
Has thoroughly examined it and found it to be highly precious,
Those who wish to be separated from the states of wandering beings
Should firmly hold to precious bodhicitta.

i.sp: the states of wandering beings
i.ev: འགྲོ་བའི་གནས་ (Skt gati-pattana) refers to the realms/destinies of rebirth: bo-shenga 1-11 འགྲོ་བ་ལྔའི་གནས་ 'the abodes of the five migrations'; bo-gyaltsab 1-11 gives འཁོར་བའི་རྒུད་པ་ 'the miseries of saṃsāra'. Here འགྲོ་བ is 'migration/destiny', not 'beings', so the locked 'wandering being' misleads.
i.fx: the realms of migration (the destinies of saṃsāra)

atts.t:
Since the sole caravan leader of wandering beings, with limitless intellect,
Has thoroughly examined it and found it to be highly precious,
Those who wish to be separated from the realms of wandering beings
Should firmly hold to precious bodhicitta.

Whether it be a father or even a mother,
Who has such a beneficial intention?
Do even the gods or the seers,
Or does even Brahmā have this?

i.sp: Do even the gods or the seers, / Or does even Brahmā have this?
i.ev: Tibetan ལྷ་དང་དྲང་སྲོང་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རུང་། ("whether gods or seers") is parallel to ཕའམ་ཡང་ན་མ་ཡང་རུང་ and takes its predicate from the next line ཚངས་པ་ལ་ཡང་འདི་ཡོད་དམ། The English turns line 3 into a verbless question ("Do even the gods or the seers") and then restarts with "Or does", which is ungrammatical as it stands; bo-kunpal 1-23 reads it as gods and seers also lacking such an intention.
i.fx:
Whether gods or seers,
Does even Brahmā have this?

atts.t:
Whether it be a father or even a mother,
Who has such a beneficial intention?
Whether gods or seers,
Does even Brahmā have this?

For those who are destitute of happiness
And who have many sufferings,
It satisfies them with all happiness
And cuts through all suffering,

i.sp: It satisfies them with all happiness / And cuts through all suffering,
i.ev: The Tibetan has no pronoun subject: the verbs ཚིམ་པ་དང་། ... གཅོད་བྱེད་ཅིང་ (continued in 1-30 by སེལ་བྱེད་པ། དེ་དང་དགེ་མཚུངས་) are nominalized actions of an unstated agent, which bo-shenga 1-29 supplies as the bodhisattva (རྒྱལ་སྲས་གང་ཞིག ... བྱམས་པ་ཆེན་པོས ... སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས) and bo-gyaltsab 1-30 as the mind (བྱེད་ལས་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་དེ). English "It" has no antecedent in the preceding verse (1-28 speaks of beings) and silently fixes one reading.
i.fx:
That which satisfies them with all happiness
And cuts through all suffering,

atts.t:
For those who are destitute of happiness
And who have many sufferings,
That which satisfies them with all happiness
And cuts through all suffering,

i.sp: That which satisfies them with all happiness
i.ev: གང་ཞིག is the agent; bo-shenga 1-29 glosses it "རྒྱལ་སྲས་གང་ཞིག" (the Victor's child, the bodhisattva) who "བདེ་བ་ཀུན་ཀྱིས་ཚིམ་པར་བྱེད་པ" and "སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྒྱུན་གཅོད་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་"; Sanskrit yaḥ is masculine/personal. "That which" leaves the subject impersonal.
i.fx: One who satisfies them with all happiness

atts.t:
To limitless numbers of sentient beings for a long time,
The unsurpassed happiness of the Sugatas,
Which fulfills all the wishes in their minds—
What need is there to mention constantly giving this?

i.sp: Which fulfills all the wishes in their minds— / What need is there to mention constantly giving this?
i.ev: In the Tibetan ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་དག་རྫོགས་བྱེད་པ། modifies རྟག་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་པ (the constant giving), as bo-kunpal 1-33 (ཡིད་ལ་གང་ཅི་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་དག་རྫོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པའི་རྟག་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་པ) and Sanskrit sakalamanoratha-sampūraṇam (accusative, agreeing with the giving) show; the English relative "Which" attaches to "the unsurpassed happiness". The honor due is to the one who gives (bo-kunpal: སྦྱིན་བདག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་བསྟོད་ཅིང་བཀུར་བར་འོས་པ་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས), which "mention constantly giving this" leaves implicit.
i.fx:
The unsurpassed happiness of the Sugatas,
Given constantly so as to fulfill all their wishes—
what need is there to mention [the honor due to one who gives thus]?

atts.t:
To limitless numbers of sentient beings for a long time,
The unsurpassed happiness of the Sugatas,
Given constantly so as to fulfill all the wishes in their minds—
What need is there to mention one who gives thus?

Taking them up with my mind, to the Sages, the supreme among beings,
Together with their children, I excellently offer them;
May those supreme worthy recipients of offerings, those of great compassion,
Think of me with love and accept these things of mine.

i.sp: the supreme among beings
i.ev: Tibetan ཐུབ་པ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱི་མཆོག; skyes bu is 'person' (not སེམས་ཅན 'beings'); bo-shenga 2-6 glosses it ཐུབ་པ་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྐང་གཉིས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག, 'supreme among persons/bipeds', and bo-kunpal 2-6 likewise སྐྱེས་བུ་རྐང་གཉིས་མི་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག. 'Beings' is the wrong register for skyes bu and could be read as all sentient beings.
i.fx: the supreme among persons

atts.t:
Taking them up with my mind, to the Sages, the supreme among persons,
Together with their children, I excellently offer them;
May those supreme worthy recipients of offerings, those of great compassion,
Think of me with love and accept these things of mine.

To the Tathāgatas and their children,
With many precious vases of scented water,
Appealing and excellently filled,
Accompanied by manifold songs and music, I offer a bath.

i.sp: Appealing and excellently filled,
i.ev: ཡིད་འོང་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ: 'filled well with (what is) pleasing'; bo-gyaltsab 2-11 reads ཡིད་དུ་འོང་བ་མེ་ཏོག་དང་བཅས་པས་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ and bo-shenga ཡིད་འོང་བས་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ, so 'pleasing' qualifies the scented water/contents, not the vases. In the English 'Appealing' dangles and reads as describing the vases.
i.fx: Well filled with what is pleasing,

atts.t:
To the Tathāgatas and their children,
With many precious vases of scented water,
Well filled with what is pleasing,
Accompanied by manifold songs and music, I offer a bath.

Their bodies, with matchless garments,
Clean and infused with supreme fragrance, I dry.
Then, to them, I offer excellently dyed,
Exceedingly fragrant, supreme robes.

i.sp: infused with supreme fragrance
i.ev: དྲི་རབ་བསྒོས་པ: རབ་ here is the intensive 'thoroughly' (Skt. pradhūpita 'well perfumed'); bo-shenga 2-12 བདུག་སྤོས་ཀྱི་དྲི་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒོས་པ, bo-gyaltsab 2-12 དྲི་ཞིམ་པོས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒོས་པ 'thoroughly scented'. 'Supreme' is not in the Tibetan.
i.fx: thoroughly perfumed

atts.t:
Their bodies, with matchless garments,
Clean and thoroughly perfumed, I dry.
Then, to them, I offer excellently dyed,
Exceedingly fragrant, supreme robes.

To the Lords of Sages, the supreme objects of offering,
With pleasing mandāra flowers and lotuses,
Blue lotuses, and all other fragrant things,
And beautifully strung, pleasing garlands, I make offerings.

i.sp: all other fragrant things
i.ev: ཨུཏྤལ་ལ་སོགས་དྲི་ཞིམ་ཐམས་ཅད: the 'fragrant (ones)' are flowers following མེ་ཏོག་; Skt. sugandhaiḥ kusumaiḥ; bo-gyaltsab 2-15 ཨུཏྤལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དྲི་ཞིམ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སིལ་མར་བྱས་པ, bo-shenga དྲི་ཞིམ་པོའི་རིགས་. 'Things' loses the restriction to flowers.
i.fx: all other fragrant flowers

atts.t:
To the Lords of Sages, the supreme objects of offering,
With pleasing mandāra flowers and lotuses,
Blue lotuses, and all other fragrant flowers,
And beautifully strung, pleasing garlands, I make offerings.

To those who reside in all directions,
The fully awakened Buddhas and those with bodhicitta,
Who possess great compassion,
Joining my palms, I pray:

i.sp: those with bodhicitta
i.ev: Here བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས is the abbreviated form of bodhisattva (Skt. bodhisattvān); bo-shenga 2-27 and bo-gyaltsab 2-27 both gloss it as བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ. The locked rendering "bodhicitta" is the mind, not the persons addressed alongside the Buddhas.
i.fx: the bodhisattvas

atts.t:
To those who reside in all directions,
The fully awakened Buddhas and bodhicitta
Who possess great compassion,
Joining my palms, I make this request:

i.sp: the fully awakened Buddhas and bodhicitta
i.ev: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་ here abbreviates བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ (bodhisattva): Sanskrit has संबुद्धान् ... बोधिसत्त्वान्; bo-shenga 2-27 reads "ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐུགས་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་མངའ་བ"; bo-gyaltsab 2-27 likewise. Those "who possess great compassion" are persons, not the mind of awakening, so the locked "bodhicitta" does not fit here.
i.fx: the fully awakened Buddhas and bodhisattvas

atts.t:
To the Three Jewels,
To parents, or to teachers and others,
Through the gateway of the afflictions, with body, speech,
And mind, whatever harm I have done,

i.sp: to teachers and others
i.ev: བླ་མ་གཞན་དག་ལ: གཞན་དག qualifies བླ་མ ("other teachers"); Skt. gurushv anyeshu; bo-kunpal 2-30 བླ་མ་གཞན་དག, bo-gyaltsab 2-30 བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་བླ་མ་གཞན་དག. English "teachers and others" can be read as teachers plus other people.
i.fx: or to other teachers

atts.t:
To the Three Jewels,
To parents, or to other teachers,
Through the gateway of the afflictions, with body, speech,
And mind, whatever harm I have done,

Without the purification of my misdeeds,
I may meet my death beforehand.
So that there is definite liberation from this,
Please protect me swiftly.

i.sp: I may meet my death beforehand
i.ev: སྔོན་དུ་འགུམ་པར་འགྱུར་དུ་མཆི states that death will come ("I am going to die"), not a possibility; bo-shenga 2-32 and bo-gyaltsab 2-32 read it as certain. "May" also reads like a wish. "Beforehand" is vague: before the misdeeds are purified (bo-kunpal 2-32 སྡིག་པ་བཤགས་པས་མ་བྱང་བར་སྔོན་དུ་འགུམ).
i.fx: I will die before that happens

i.sp: from this
i.ev: འདི་ལས is explicitly "from this misdeed" in bo-kunpal 2-32 (སྡིག་པ་འདི་ལས) and bo-shenga 2-32 (སྡིག་པ་འདི་ལས); the English "this" has no clear referent (it could be death).
i.fx: from these misdeeds

atts.t:
Without the purification of my misdeeds,
I will die before that happens.
So that there is definite liberation from these misdeeds,
Please protect me swiftly.

This Lord of Death cannot be trusted;
He does not wait for what is done or not done.
Whether sick or healthy,
No one can trust this fleeting life.

i.sp: this fleeting life
i.ev: གློ་བུར་ཚེ means life that ends suddenly/unexpectedly (Skt. ākasmika); bo-kunpal 2-33 གློ་བུར་ཉིད་དུ་མི་འཆི་བའི་ངེས་པ་མེད, bo-shenga 2-33 གློ་བུར་བའི་ཚེ, bo-gyaltsab 2-33 གློ་བུར་དུ་འཆི་བ. "Fleeting" means brief, not sudden or unpredictable.
i.fx: this life, which can end suddenly

atts.t:
This Lord of Death cannot be trusted;
He does not wait for what is done or not done.
Whether sick or healthy,
No one can trust this life, which can end suddenly.

Even a person being led today
To a place where their limbs will be severed is terrified;
With a parched mouth, distressed eyes, and the like,
They appear transformed from how they were before.

i.sp: They appear transformed from how they were before.
i.ev: The Tibetan ends སྔ་ལས་གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་སྣང་ན། with the conditional ན, confirmed by bo-kunpal 2-43 (…གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཉམས་ཐག་པར་སྣང༷་ན༷།) and bo-shenga 2-43 (…འགྱུར་བར་སྣང་ན།). The verse is the protasis to 2-44 (…སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས), so the English makes it a standalone assertion and leaves 2-44's 'what need to mention' without its antecedent.
i.fx: If they appear transformed from how they were before, (what need to mention ... [2-44])

atts.t:
Even a person being led today
To a place where their limbs will be severed is terrified;
With a parched mouth, distressed eyes, and the like,
If they appear transformed from how they were before,

What need to mention the utter misery
Of one seized by the messengers of Yama
With their terrifying physical forms,
And stricken by the great disease of terror?

i.sp: the great disease of terror
i.ev: འཇིགས་ཆེན་ནད་ = 'disease of great terror'; bo-shenga 2-44 glosses འཇིགས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ནད་ཀྱིས། and Sanskrit mahātrāsajvara. The English attaches 'great' to the disease rather than to the terror.
i.fx: the disease of great terror

atts.t:
Seized by the messengers of Yama
With their terrifying physical forms,
And stricken by the disease of great terror,
What need to mention their utter misery?

i.sp: their utter misery
i.ev: The helpless one is the person seized and stricken (bo-shenga 2-44 "བཟུང་བར་གྱུར་ཅིང་... ཐེབས་པར་གྱུར་པ་ན། རབ་ཏུ་ཉམ་ཐག་པར་འགྱུར་བ"; bo-gyaltsab 2-44 "བཟུང་བར་གྱུར་ཅིང་... རབ་ཏུ་ཉམ་ཐག་པ"), not the messengers of Yama. In the English, "their" has no antecedent but the messengers, so it can be read as their misery.
i.fx: the utter helplessness of one so seized and stricken

atts.t:
Even when frightened by an ordinary illness,
If one must act according to the physician's words,
Of a hundred faults, such as desire,
When constantly stricken by their disease, what need to mention?

i.sp:
Of a hundred faults, such as desire,
When constantly stricken by their disease, what need to mention?
i.ev: Tibetan འདོད་ཆགས་ལ་སོགས་ཉེས་པ་བརྒྱའི། ནད་ཀྱིས་རྟག་བཏབ་ = 'constantly afflicted by the disease of a hundred faults such as desire' (bo-shenga 2-54: ཉེས་པ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ཡི། ནད་ཀྱིས་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་བཏབ་པ). The English fronts 'Of a hundred faults' so that it reads as the thing 'to mention', obscuring that the faults are the disease.
i.fx: When one is constantly stricken by the disease of a hundred faults such as desire, what need to mention?

atts.t:
Even when frightened by an ordinary illness,
If one must act according to the physician's words,
When one is constantly stricken by the disease
Of a hundred faults such as desire, what need to mention?

For all sentient beings, in the virtue
That brings rest from the suffering of the lower realms, and
In those with suffering abiding in happiness,
With joy I rejoice.

i.sp: For all sentient beings, in the virtue
i.ev: Tibetan 'སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་ངན་སོང་གི། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ངལ་སོའི་དགེ་བ་' has 'ཀུན་གྱི' (genitive), not a benefactive: it is the virtue/suffering belonging to all beings, not a rejoicing 'for' them. Sanskrit 'sarvasattvaiḥ kṛtaṃ śubham' = virtue done by all beings; bo-shenga 3-1 'སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ཀྱི་... དགེ་བ་བཅུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པ'; bo-gyaltsab 3-1 'སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་ངན་སོང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ངལ་གསོ་ཞིང་... དགེ་བ་'.
i.fx: In the virtue of all sentient beings that brings rest from the suffering of the lower realms,

atts.t:
In the virtue of all sentient beings
That brings rest from the suffering of the lower realms,
And in suffering beings abiding in happiness,
With joy I rejoice.

i.sp:
In the virtue of all sentient beings
That brings rest from the suffering of the lower realms
i.ev: Tibetan སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་ངན་སོང་གི། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ངལ་སོའི་དགེ་བ: the genitive ཀུན་གྱི་ binds 'all sentient beings' to the lower-realm suffering. bo-gyaltsab 3-1 glosses འཁོར་བར་གནས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་ངན་སོང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ངལ་གསོ་ཞིང་... འཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་རྒྱུའི་དགེ་བ (virtue that gives all beings rest from their lower-realm suffering); bo-shenga likewise. The English makes the virtue 'of' the beings and leaves unstated whose suffering is relieved.
i.fx:
In the virtue that gives all sentient beings rest
From the suffering of the lower realms

atts.t:
To the Buddhas of all directions,
I join my palms and pray:
For sentient beings confused in the darkness of suffering,
Please light the lamp of the Dharma.

i.sp: confused in the darkness of suffering
i.ev: Tibetan 'སེམས་ཅན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མུན་འཐོམས་ལ།'. Commentaries read suffering and the darkness as separate: bo-shenga 3-4 'སེམས་ཅན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་ཤེས་པའི་མུན་པར་འཐོམས་པ' and bo-gyaltsab 3-4 'སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཞིང་མ་རིག་པའི་མུན་པར་འཐོམས་པ' (suffering and bewildered in the darkness of ignorance). Sanskrit 'mohād duḥkhaprapātinām'. The darkness is ignorance, not suffering.
i.fx: For sentient beings who suffer and are bewildered in the darkness [of ignorance],

atts.t:
To the Buddhas of all directions,
I join my palms and pray:
For sentient beings suffering and bewildered in darkness,
Please light the lamp of the Dharma.

A child of the Victors, in that way,
Having firmly taken hold of bodhicitta,
Always and without wavering,
Should strive not to transgress the trainings.

i.sp: without wavering
i.ev: གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར; bo-shenga 4-1 glosses it 'ལེ་ལོའི་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར' (without the negligence/slackness of laziness) and Sanskrit has 'atandritaḥ' (unslothful); bo-gyaltsab 4-1 'སེམས་སྐད་ཅིག་ཀྱང་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར'. 'Wavering' suggests irresolution, not lapse or negligence.
i.fx: without lapse

atts.t:
A child of the Victors, in that way,
Having firmly taken hold of bodhicitta,
Always and without lapse,
Should strive not to transgress the trainings.

i.sp: without lapse
i.ev: གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར is "without distraction/slackness": bo-shenga 4-1 "ལེ་ལོའི་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར"; bo-gyaltsab 4-1 "སེམས་སྐད་ཅིག་ཀྱང་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར". "Lapse" is vague and could be read as lapsing in the trainings, which blurs it with "not transgress".
i.fx: without distraction (or laxity)

atts.t:
If, having promised in that way,
I do not accomplish it through action,
By deceiving all those sentient beings,
What sort of wandering being will I become?

i.sp: what sort of wandering being will I become
i.ev: བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ་ཅི་འདྲར་འགྱུར: here འགྲོ་བ is the destiny/course (Skt 'kā gatir me'), not a being; bo-gyaltsab 4-4 'བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ་ཇི་འདྲར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ངན་འགྲོར་འགྲོ་བ་ལས་མ་འདས་པའོ' and bo-shenga 4-4 treat it as the realm of rebirth. The locked 'wandering being' is applied mechanically and distorts the sense.
i.fx: what will my destiny be?

atts.t:
If, having promised in this way,
I do not accomplish it through action,
having deceived all those sentient beings,
what kind of wandering being will I become?

i.sp: what kind of wandering being will I become?
i.ev: བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ here is "my destiny / where I go" (Sanskrit का गतिर्मे, "what destination for me"), not a type of being. bo-shenga 4-4 "སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་ལས་གཞན་གྱི་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་དོ"; bo-gyaltsab 4-4 "བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ་ཇི་འདྲར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ངན་འགྲོར་འགྲོ་བ་ལས་མ་འདས་པ"; bo-kunpal 4-4 "དམྱལ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངན་འགྲོར་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར". The locked "wandering being" (beings) is misapplied to the rebirth-destiny sense.
i.fx: what will my destiny be? (what rebirth state will be mine?)

atts.t:
For a bodhisattva, this
Is the heaviest among downfalls,
Because should it occur,
The welfare of all sentient beings is diminished.

i.sp: The welfare of all sentient beings is diminished.
i.ev: སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་དམན: the bodhisattva falls short in regard to beings' welfare; bo-kunpal 4-8 'སེམས་ཅན་མ་ལུས་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་ནུས་པ་དམན་པར་འགྱུར་བ' and bo-gyaltsab 4-8 'གཞན་དོན་གྱི་བསམ་པ་ཉམས་པས...' show it is the bodhisattva's capacity to benefit beings that diminishes, not the beings' welfare as such.
i.fx: one falls short in accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.

atts.t:
For a bodhisattva, this
Is the heaviest among downfalls,
Because should it occur,
One falls short in accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.

If anyone else, even for a single moment,
Creates an obstacle to this merit,
Since the welfare of sentient beings is diminished,
Their lower realms will be endless.

i.sp:
Creates an obstacle to this merit,
Since the welfare of sentient beings is diminished,
i.ev: འདིའི་བསོད་ནམས: 'this' refers to this bodhisattva (bo-shenga 4-9 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདིའི་བསོད་ནམས'; bo-gyaltsab 4-9). Line 3 (སེམས་ཅན་དོན་ལ་དམན་གྱུར་པས) is that the bodhisattva's ability to benefit beings is diminished (bo-gyaltsab 4-9 'ནུས་པ་དམན་པར་གྱུར་པར་བྱས་པས'); the English leaves the possessor of the merit and the thing diminished unclear.
i.fx: Creates an obstacle to this bodhisattva's merit, / Since he is left falling short in the welfare of sentient beings,

atts.t:
If anyone else, even for a single moment,
Creates an obstacle to this bodhisattva's merit,
Since he is left falling short in the welfare of sentient beings,
Their lower realms will be endless.

i.sp: Since he is left falling short in the welfare of sentient beings, / Their lower realms will be endless.
i.ev: The Tibetan subject of དམན་གྱུར་པས is the bodhisattva (བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ in line 2), whose capacity is diminished; bo-shenga 4-9: "རྒྱལ་བའི་སྲས་དེ་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པ་ལ་དམན་པར་གྱུར་པས། གེགས་བྱེད་པ་པོ་དེ་ཡི་ངན་འགྲོ་ལ་མུ་དང་མཐའ་མེད". English "he" is followed by "Their" and so can be read as the obstructor. Also ངན་འགྲོ is a single rebirth-state (Skt durgatiparyanto), the obstructor's, not plural realms.
i.fx: Since that bodhisattva is left falling short in the welfare of sentient beings, / The obstructer's lower realm has no end.

atts.t:
Even the happiness of a single sentient being,
If destroying it leads to one's own ruin,
Limitless as the entirety of space,
What need to speak of destroying the happiness of embodied beings?

i.sp: Limitless as the entirety of space,
i.ev: ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི་ལུས་ཅན: the embodied beings extend to the limits of all space (Skt 'aśeṣākāśaparyanta-vāsinām'; bo-gyaltsab 4-10 'ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་པའི་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི་ལུས་ཅན'). The English turns this into a comparison ('as limitless as space') that is not in the text.
i.fx: Embodied beings who pervade all of space to its limits,

atts.t:
Even the happiness of a single sentient being,
If destroying it leads to my own ruin,
For those who pervade all of space to its limits,
What need to speak of destroying the happiness of embodied beings?

i.sp: For those who pervade all of space to its limits, / What need to speak of destroying the happiness of embodied beings?
i.ev: Tibetan "ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི། ལུས་ཅན" is an attributive on ལུས་ཅན: embodied beings who extend to (dwell to) the limits of all space (Skt aśeṣākāśaparyanta-vāsinām; bo-gyaltsab 4-10: "ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་པའི་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི་ལུས་ཅན"). The English makes line 3 a dangling "For those who..." that detaches from "embodied beings" and uses "pervade", which the Tibetan/Sanskrit do not say.
i.fx: Of embodied beings dwelling to the limits of all space, / What need to speak of destroying their happiness?

atts.t:
If I have not practiced virtues,
And have accumulated misdeeds,
For even a hundred million eons,
I will not hear even the sound of the happy realms.

i.sp: a hundred million eons
i.ev: བསྐལ་པ་བྱེ་བ་བརྒྱ: བྱེ་བ is ten million (Skt koṭi), so བྱེ་བ་བརྒྱ (kalpakoṭiśata) is a hundred ten-millions, i.e. a billion, not a hundred million.
i.fx: a hundred koṭis (ten millions) of eons

atts.t:
If I have not practiced virtues,
And have accumulated misdeeds,
For even a hundred ten-million eons,
I will not hear even the sound of the happy realms.

If even a misdeed committed in a single instant
Leads to dwelling in the Avīci hell for an eon,
Due to the misdeeds accumulated in beginningless saṃsāra,
What need is there to mention that I will not go to a happy realm?

i.sp: that I will not go
i.ev: The Tibetan བདག་གི་/subject is absent: "བདེ་འགྲོར་མི་འགྲོ་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས" has no first-person subject (Shenga 4-21: "བདེ་འགྲོར་མི་འགྲོ་བ་ནི་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས"), and the Sanskrit "kā sugatau kathā" is likewise impersonal. The English adds "I".
i.fx: that one will not go to a happy realm

atts.t:
If even a misdeed committed in a single instant
Leads to dwelling in the Avīci hell for an eon,
Due to the misdeeds accumulated in beginningless saṃsāra,
What need is there to mention that one will not go to a happy realm?

Having experienced just that much,
One will not attain liberation,
Because while experiencing it in this way,
Other misdeeds are fully generated.

i.sp: One will not attain liberation
i.ev: Commentaries gloss རྣམ་ཐར་མི་འགྱུར as not being freed from that suffering / the lower realms: bo-shenga 4-22 "སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་བར་མི་འགྱུར", bo-kunpal 4-22 "ངན་སོང་གི་གནས་དེ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་མི་འགྱུར". "Attain liberation" suggests final liberation.
i.fx: One will not be liberated from it

atts.t:
Having experienced just that much,
One will not attain liberation,
For while experiencing it,
Other misdeeds are fully produced.

i.sp: One will not attain liberation,
i.ev: རྣམ་ཐར་མི་འགྱུར་ is "will not be released/freed" from the suffering of the lower realm (Skt na vimucyate). bo-gyaltsab 4-22: "ངན་འགྲོ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ"; bo-kunpal 4-22: "ངན་སོང་གི་གནས་དེ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་མི་འགྱུར"; bo-shenga: "སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་བར་མི་འགྱུར". "Attain liberation" turns release from that state into attaining the goal of liberation.
i.fx: One will not be liberated [from it],

atts.t:
The enemies of hatred, craving, and so forth,
Have no hands, feet, and so forth,
And are neither brave nor wise; yet how is it
That they have made me like a slave?

i.sp: The enemies of hatred, craving, and so forth
i.ev: Tibetan "ཞེ་སྡང་སྲེད་སོགས་དགྲ་རྣམས" means the enemies that are hatred, craving, etc. (Shenga 4-28 "ཞེ་སྡང་དང་སྲེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགྲ་བོ་རྣམས"; Sanskrit tṛṣṇādveṣādiśatravaḥ). "Enemies of hatred" reads as a genitive of opposition.
i.fx: The enemies, hatred, craving, and so forth,

atts.t:
The enemies, hatred, craving, and so forth,
Have no hands, feet, and so forth,
And are neither brave nor wise; yet how is it
That they have made me like a slave?

Thus, as long as I do not manifestly
And certainly destroy this enemy, I shall not forsake my effort here.
Becoming angered by even a slight, temporary harm,
Those full of pride do not sleep until they have destroyed it.

i.sp: a slight, temporary harm ... until they have destroyed it
i.ev: "གནོད་བྱེད་ཆུང་ངུ" is a slight harm-doer (an enemy), not "harm"; "རེ་ཞིག" means "to begin with / for instance", not "temporary". Gyaltsab 4-36: "གནོད་བྱེད་ཆུང་དུ་ཚིག་རྩུབ་ཙམ་སྨྲ་བ་ལ་ཡང་ཁྲོས་པར་གྱུར་པ ... དགྲ་དེ་མ་བཅོམ་པར" and Kunpal 4-36 "ཐ་མལ་པའི་དགྲ་བོ ... གནོད་བྱེད་ཆུང་ངུ་ཙམ་ལ་ཡང་". What is destroyed is the enemy, not the harm.
i.fx: For instance, those swollen with pride, angered even by a slight wrongdoer, do not sleep until they have destroyed that enemy.

atts.t:
Thus, as long as I do not manifestly
And certainly destroy this enemy, I shall not forsake my effort here.
For instance, angered even by a slight wrongdoer,
Those swollen with pride do not sleep until they have destroyed that enemy.

These afflictions, who suffer through natural death—
If, when arrayed in battle, even those who fiercely desire to destroy them
Disregard the suffering of being struck by arrows, spears, and weapons,
And do not turn back and flee without accomplishing their goal,

i.sp: These afflictions, who suffer through natural death
i.ev: Here ཉོན་མོངས is not the mental afflictions but a disparaging word for ordinary, pitiable enemies who die naturally anyway: bo-kunpal 4-37 "དགྲ་བོ་ཐ་མལ་པ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཞེས་སྨད་པའི་ཚིག་སྟེ་ཉམས་ཐག་ཅིང་སྙིང་རྗེ་བའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་དགྲ་བོ་འདི་དག"; bo-shenga 4-37 "ཉོན་མོངས་ཏེ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དག"; Gyaltsab 4-38 glosses them as the foe in battle (ཕ་རོལ). The warriors in the simile fight such foes, then 4-38 draws the contrast with the real enemy. Rendering them "afflictions" collapses simile and application.
i.fx: These wretched foes (called kleśa, "afflicted ones", here as a term of pity), who suffer through natural death

atts.t:
Those afflictions subjected to suffering by natural death—
If even those who desire to forcefully destroy them when arrayed in battle,
Having disregarded the suffering of being struck by arrows, spears, and weapons,
Do not turn back and flee without accomplishing their goal,

i.sp: Those afflictions subjected to suffering by natural death—
i.ev: Here ཉོན་མོངས་ is not the mental afflictions but a word of pity for the ordinary enemies of the battle simile. bo-kunpal 4-37: དགྲ་བོ་ཐ་མལ་པ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཞེས་སྨད་པའི་ཚིག་སྟེ་ཉམས་ཐག་ཅིང་སྙིང་རྗེ་བའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་དགྲ་བོ་འདི་དག (ordinary enemies, 'wretched', objects of pity); bo-shenga 4-37: ཉོན་མོངས་ཏེ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དག. The mental afflictions are the target only of the application in the following verse. Rendering with the locked term 'afflictions' gives the wrong referent and collapses simile and application.
i.fx: Those wretched enemies, made to suffer by their very nature as mortals who must die,

atts.t:
Those wretched enemies made to suffer by natural death—
If even those who desire to forcefully destroy them when arrayed in battle,
Having disregarded the suffering of being struck by arrows, spears, and weapons,
Do not turn back and flee without accomplishing their goal,

If even the scars inflicted by meaningless enemies
Are worn like ornaments upon the body,
For me, who perfectly strives to accomplish the great purpose,
Why should suffering be a harm?

i.sp: the scars inflicted by meaningless enemies
i.ev: "དོན་མེད་" qualifies the purposeless infliction of wounds, not the enemies: Gyaltsab 4-39 "དོན་མེད་པ་དགོས་པ་ཆུང་ངུའི་ཆེད་དུ་ལུས་ལ་དགྲ་ཡིས་རྨ་སྲོལ་བཏོད་པ"; Sanskrit akāraṇena riputkṣatāni.
i.fx: the scars that enemies inflict for no meaningful purpose

atts.t:
If even the scars that enemies inflict for no meaningful purpose
Are worn like ornaments upon the body,
For me, who perfectly strives to accomplish the great purpose,
Why should suffering be a harm?

Reaching the ends of space in the ten directions,
To liberate wandering beings from afflictions,
When I promised this, I myself
Was not freed from afflictions.

i.sp: Reaching the ends of space in the ten directions,
i.ev: The Tibetan ཕྱོགས་བཅུ་ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པའི། is a genitive modifier of འགྲོ་བ (beings who extend to the ends of space; Skt daśadigvyomaparyanta-jagat; bo-kunpal 4-41 ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པར་ཁྱབ་པའི་འགྲོ་བ). In the English the opening participial phrase dangles and can be read as describing the speaker or the act of liberating.
i.fx: To liberate from afflictions the wandering beings who reach to the ends of space in the ten directions,

atts.t:
To liberate from afflictions the wandering beings
Who reach to the ends of space in the ten directions,
When I promised this, I myself
Was not freed from afflictions.

i.sp: When I promised this, I myself / Was not freed from afflictions.
i.ev: མ་གྲོལ་བ is a state continuing at the time of the vow and now, not a completed past event: bo-shenga 4-41 "གང་ཚེ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་...ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམས་ལས་མ་གྲོལ་ན"; bo-kunpal "ཉོན་མོངས་པ་རྣམས་ལས་ཅུང་ཟད་ཙམ་ཡང་མ་གྲོལ་བར་གནས་ན". The verse is a clause continuing into the next verse. The English past finite "Was not freed" closes it as a past statement.
i.fx: When I promised this, I myself / Was still not free from afflictions,

atts.t:
I shall be attached to this,
And, holding a grudge, engage in battle;
Afflictions of such a kind
Are excepted, as they destroy afflictions.

i.sp: Are excepted, as they destroy afflictions.
i.ev: The Tibetan ཉོན་མོངས་འཇོམས་བྱེད་མ་གཏོགས་སོ། leaves implicit what the exception is from; bo-gyaltsab 4-43 and bo-shenga 4-43 make it explicit: such seeming afflictions, being what destroys afflictions, are excepted from what is to be abandoned (སྤང་བྱར་མ་གཏོགས་སོ). English "excepted" alone does not say from what.
i.fx: Are excepted from what is to be abandoned, since they destroy afflictions.

atts.t:
I shall be attached to this,
And, holding a grudge, engage in battle;
Afflictions of such a kind
Are excepted from what is to be abandoned, since they destroy afflictions.

Even if I am burned and killed,
Or even if my head is severed, it is better;
I shall never, in any circumstance,
Bow down to the enemies, the afflictions.

i.sp: it is better
i.ev: བླའི། (Skt kāmam, "so be it / let it be") is a concession, not a comparative. bo-kunpal 4-44 glosses it སླ་ཞིང་ ("easy / no matter") and bo-gyaltsab 4-44 says that being burned or beheaded only discards the body of this life, i.e. is of little consequence. "It is better" asserts a preference the Tibetan does not state.
i.fx: so be it

atts.t:
Even if I am burned and killed,
Or even if my head is severed, so be it;
I shall never, in any circumstance,
Bow down to the enemies, the afflictions.

Afflictions, wretched afflictions, are abandoned by the eye of wisdom;
Expelled from my mind, where will they go?
Where will they dwell, to return and harm me?
It is only that I, being weak-minded, lack effort.

i.sp: are abandoned by the eye of wisdom
i.ev: ཤེས་རབ་མིག་གིས་སྤང་། is an exhortation/gerundive (Skt prajñādṛṣṭisādhyā "to be overcome by the eye of wisdom"); bo-shenga 4-46 has སྤང་བར་བྱ་སྟེ ("are to be abandoned"). The indicative passive states as fact what the verse prescribes.
i.fx: are to be abandoned by the eye of wisdom

atts.t:
Afflictions, wretched afflictions, are to be abandoned by the eye of wisdom;
Expelled from my mind, where will they go?
Where will they dwell, to return and harm me?
It is only that I, being weak-minded, lack effort.

Tigers, lions, elephants, bears,
Snakes, and all enemies,
Hell guardians of the hell of sentient beings,
Sorcerers, and likewise rākṣasas—

i.sp: Hell guardians of the hell of sentient beings
i.ev: སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བའི་སྲུང་མ is the locked "hell guardian" (Skt narakapālāḥ; bo-kunpal 5-4 explains them as Yama's agents in hell). Here སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ is simply "hell"; rendering the second locked entry inside the first produces a redundant, odd phrase.
i.fx: Hell guardians

i.sp: Sorcerers
i.ev: བྱད་མ (Skt ḍākinī) is not a human sorcerer: bo-kunpal 5-4 describes it as a spirit/revenant incited by another's power (བྱད་མ་གདོན་རྦད་འདྲེ་རྦོད་གཏོང), and bo-gyaltsab 5-5 glosses བྱད་མ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་མ, harming through mantra.
i.fx: Witches (ḍākinīs)

atts.t:
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears,
Snakes, and all enemies,
Hell guardians, and
Witches, and likewise rākṣasas—

i.sp: Witches
i.ev: བྱད་མ is glossed by bo-kunpal 5-4 as "ཕ་རོལ་པོའི་མཐུས་རྦད་པའི་བྱད་མ་གདོན་རྦད་འདྲེ་རྦོད་གཏོང": harmful spirits/hexes sent by another's power, not human witches. "Witches" (Skt ḍākinyaḥ) suggests human sorceresses.
i.fx: Hex-sent spirits (byad ma)

atts.t:
Thus, all fears and
Immeasurable sufferings too
Arise from the mind;
So the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.

i.sp: So the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.
i.ev: The last line (ཡང་དག་གསུང་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན།) reports the source of the claim in line 3 (བྱུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས། "that they arise from the mind"); it is not a consequence. "So" suggests a conclusion drawn from the preceding lines; Skt yasmāt ... kathitam gives the reasoning as "since ... as taught".
i.fx: as the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.

atts.t:
Thus, all fears and
Immeasurable sufferings too
Arise from the mind,
As the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.

i.sp: Thus, all fears and
i.ev: འདི་ལྟར here introduces the reason for the preceding claim (Skt yasmāt "since"); bo-gyaltsab 5-6: "རྒྱུ་མཚན་འདི་ལྟར། ཚེ་འདི་དང་ཕྱི་མའི་འཇིགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་...སེམས་ཉིད་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ཡིན". English "Thus" reads as a conclusion drawn from what precedes, reversing the direction of the argument.
i.fx: For all fears and

atts.t:
The weapons of the hell of sentient beings,
Who intentionally created them?
Who created the burning iron ground?
From what did those masses of fire arise?

i.sp: From what did those masses of fire arise?
i.ev: The Tibetan text as given reads མེ་ཚོགས, which the English follows, but bo-gyaltsab 5-8 states that མེ་ཚོགས is a corrupt reading in some editions; Skt striyaḥ and the other readings (bo-gyaltsab 5-7 མོ་ཚོགས; bo-kunpal མོ་ཡི་ཚོགས; bo-shenga on the shalmali tree) mean the groups of women in hell.
i.fx: From what did those groups of women arise? (with a note on the variant མེ་ཚོགས "masses of fire")

atts.t:
The weapons of the hell of sentient beings,
Who intentionally created them?
Who created the burning iron ground?
From what did those groups of women arise?

i.sp: From what did those groups of women arise?
i.ev: The Tibetan as given reads "མེ་ཚོགས" (masses of fire), which bo-shenga 5-7 follows ("མེ་ཚོགས་དེ་དག་རྒྱུ་ཅི་ལས་བྱུང་"). The English follows the variant "མོ་ཚོགས" (bo-kunpal "མོ་ཡི་ཚོགས"; bo-gyaltsab 5-8 calls མེ་ཚོགས a corrupt reading; Skt striyaḥ). English does not render the Tibetan as given, so the textual choice should be marked.
i.fx: From what did those groups of women (var. masses of fire) arise?

atts.t:
All such things as these
Were taught by the Sage to be the mind of misdeed.
Thus, in the three worlds,
There is no fear other than the mind.

i.sp: Were taught by the Sage to be the mind of misdeed.
i.ev: སྡིག་སེམས་ཡིན་པར ... གསུངས། is elliptical: the commentaries read it as arising from or caused by the mind of misdeed (Skt pāpacittasamudbhūtam; bo-kunpal 5-8 སྡིག་པ་མི་དགེ་བའི་སེམས་གོམས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བྱུང་བ; bo-shenga 5-8 སེམས་ཉིད་དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན). "To be the mind of misdeed" reads as identity.
i.fx: Were taught by the Sage to be (products of) the mind of misdeed.

atts.t:
All such things as these
Were taught by the Sage to arise from the mind of misdeed.
Thus, in the three worlds,
There is no fear other than the mind.

Whatever the result of generating a single clear mind,
Such as Brahmā and so forth,
The result of body and speech, too,
Because of weak conduct, is not like that.

i.sp: The result of body and speech, too,
i.ev: Tibetan ལུས་ངག་བཅས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང་ = the result [of effort] 'accompanied by' body and speech, even so. Sanskrit sahāpi vākśarīrābhyām ('even together with speech and body'); bo-kunpal 5-15 ལུས་ངག་དང་བཅས་པའི་འབད་རྩོལ་ཆེན་པོས; bo-gyaltsab 5-15 ལུས་ངག་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང༌། The English drops བཅས་པ ('together with') and so reads body and speech alone as the source.
i.fx: The result, even when accompanied by body and speech,

atts.t:
Whatever the result of generating a single clear mind,
Such as Brahmā and so forth,
The result, even when accompanied by body and speech,
Because of weak conduct, is not like that.

i.sp: Whatever the result of generating a single clear mind, / Such as Brahmā and so forth,
i.ev: Tibetan "འབྲས་བུ་གང་། ཚངས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡིན་པ་ལྟར" means: just as the result of generating a single clear mind is (rebirth as) Brahmā etc. Brahmā is the result, not an example of a mind, and the comparison marker ལྟར is lost; bo-shenga 5-15: "འབྲས་བུ་གང་། ཚངས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གནས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡིན་པ་ལྟར". "Such as" makes the lines read as a list of examples of results/minds.
i.fx: Just as the result of generating a single clear mind / Is [rebirth as] Brahmā and so forth,

atts.t:
Having thought in this way, with shame,
Respect, and fear, one should bear it in mind.
Therefore, the recollection of the Buddha
Will also arise in one again and again.

i.sp: one should bear it in mind
i.ev: དེ་བཞིན་གནོས (mnos) is "undertake/take on likewise"; bo-kunpal 5-32 glosses དེ་བཞིན་དུ་མནོས་ཏེ་གནས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག ("having so undertaken, remain"), Sanskrit tathā tiṣṭhet "remain thus". "Bear it in mind" adds an object ("it") and drops the དེ་བཞིན "thus/likewise" that links back to the shame, respect and fear.
i.fx: one should thus take it on and remain so

atts.t:
Having thought in this way, with shame,
Respect, and fear, one should thus take it on and remain so.
Therefore, the recollection of the Buddha
Will also arise in one again and again.

First, having recognized a mind such as this
To be faulty,
At that time I, like a piece of wood,
Should remain steadfast.

i.sp: like a piece of wood
i.ev: ཤིང་བཞིན་ is rendered "like a log of wood" in the glossary and in 5-48, 5-50, 5-51; here the same phrase ཤིང་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་ is rendered "like a piece of wood", an unmotivated inconsistency (bo-kunpal 5-34 likens it to a great tree stump unmoved by wind).
i.fx: like a log of wood

atts.t:
First, having recognized a mind such as this
To be faulty,
At that time I, like a log of wood,
Should remain steadfast.

Having prepared for an action with the thought,
"My body shall remain like this,"
One should then occasionally look,
Asking, "How is this body remaining?"

i.sp: Having prepared for an action
i.ev: བྱ་བ་བསྡོགས་ནས is glossed by bo-shenga 5-39 as བརྩམས་པར་བྱས་ནས ("having begun/set about") and by bo-kunpal 5-39 as བྱ་བ་དེའི་མགོ་བརྩམས་པ ("having begun that action"); Sanskrit kriyām ākṣipya. The action is already started, not merely prepared for.
i.fx: Having set about an action with the thought,

atts.t:
Having set about an action with the thought,
"My body shall remain like this,"
One should then occasionally look,
Asking, "How is this body remaining?"

So that the mad elephant of the mind
Does not escape from how it is bound
To the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma,
One should examine with all effort.

i.sp: Does not escape from how it is bound
i.ev: ཇི་ལྟར་བཏགས་པ་མི་འཆོར་བར། དེ་ལྟར་འབད་པ་ཀུན་གྱིས་བརྟག is a ji-ltar...de-ltar clause: as bound, it does not escape (bo-gyaltsab 5-40: ཇི་ལྟར་བཏགས་པ་མི་འཆོར་བར་). "Escape from how it is bound" is hard to parse and suggests escaping a manner of binding, not escaping the pillar.
i.fx: So that the mad elephant of the mind, once tied to the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma, does not escape

atts.t:
So that the mad elephant of the mind,
Once tied to the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma,
Does not escape,
One should thus examine with all effort.

If one digs the earth or cuts grass without purpose,
Or draws lines on the ground and so forth,
Having remembered the training of the Sugatas,
One should, out of fear, instantly abandon them.

i.sp: the training of the Sugatas
i.ev: བདེ་གཤེགས་བསླབ་པ has no plural marker; bo-gyaltsab 5-46 has བདེ་གཤེགས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ and bo-shenga བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པའི་བསླབ་པ (singular); Sanskrit tāthāgatīṃ śikṣām is singular.
i.fx: the training of the Sugata

atts.t:
If one digs the earth or cuts grass without purpose,
Or draws lines on the ground and so forth,
Having remembered the training of the Sugata,
One should, out of fear, instantly abandon them.

Forsaking the welfare of others,
And desiring to pursue my own welfare,
Or if a mind desiring to speak arises,
Then I should remain like a log of wood.

i.sp: Forsaking the welfare of others, / And desiring to pursue my own welfare, / Or if a mind desiring to speak arises
i.ev: Tibetan: གཞན་དོན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བ་དང་། རང་དོན་གཉེར་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་། སྨྲ་བར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་ན། — three parallel items joined by དང་ all governed by one སེམས་བྱུང་ན ("if a mind ... arises"); bo-gyaltsab 5-52: ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བའམ། རང་དོན་གཉེར་བར་འདོད་པ་དག་དང་། ངག་སྨྲ་བར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་ན. The English leaves "Forsaking" and "desiring" as dangling participles with no subject and switches to "Or if" for the last item, so the syntax of the three clauses is unclear.
i.fx: If a mind arises that forsakes the welfare of others, desires to pursue my own welfare, or desires to speak,

atts.t:
If a mind arises that forsakes the welfare of others,
Desires to pursue my own welfare,
Or desires to speak,
Then I should remain like a log of wood.

Do not be disheartened by the mutually discordant
Desires of childish ones,
But thinking, "Due to the arising of their afflictions,
This mind has arisen," be a compassionate one.

i.sp: Due to the arising of their afflictions, / This mind has arisen
i.ev: Tibetan: ཉོན་མོངས་སྐྱེས་པ་འདི་དག་གི། སེམས་འདི་བྱུང་སྙམ — the genitive འདི་དག་གི ("of these [beings]") governs སེམས་འདི ("this mind"); bo-gyaltsab 5-56: འདི་དག་གི་སེམས་འདི་བྱུང་བས; bo-kunpal: བྱིས་པ་འདི་དག་གི་ ... སེམས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ ... བྱུང་བའོ་སྙམ. In the English "their" modifies only "afflictions", so "this mind" could be read as the practitioner's own mind.
i.fx: "Because afflictions have arisen in them, this mind of theirs has arisen,"

atts.t:
Do not be disheartened by the mutually discordant
Desires of childish ones,
But thinking, "Because afflictions have arisen in them,
This mind of theirs has arisen," be a compassionate one.

By vultures craving flesh,
Even when dragged back and forth everywhere,
If you, O mind, are not displeased,
Why do you care for it now?

i.sp: Even when dragged back and forth everywhere ... Why do you care for it now?
i.ev: The Tibetan elides the object (the corpse/body); bo-shenga 5-59 and bo-gyaltsab 5-59 supply it: ལུས་དེ་ ... བཤལ་ཅིང་ཁྲིད་ཀྱང་ ... ལུས་ལ་ཆགས་ནས་ཁ་ཏ་བྱེད. The English gives no antecedent for the dragged thing or for "it", and the preceding verse (5-58) concerns the mind, so "it" is likely to be misread.
i.fx: Even when [the body] is dragged back and forth everywhere ... Why do you now care for [it]?

atts.t:
By vultures craving flesh,
Even when the body is dragged back and forth everywhere,
If you, O mind, are not displeased,
Why do you now care for it?

One should speak of good qualities in private,
And if good qualities are spoken of, join in.
If one's own good qualities are spoken of,
One should understand that as them knowing good qualities.

i.sp: in private
i.ev: ལྐོག་ན་ཡོན་ཏན་བརྗོད་བྱ་ཞིང་ = praise 'behind their back / in their absence' (Sanskrit parokṣam). bo-kunpal 5-76: ལྐོག་ན་འང་དེའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གཞན་ལ་བརྗོད་པས་བསྟོད་པར་བྱ, to avoid the suspicion of flattery (ཁ་གསག); bo-shenga 5-76 same. 'In private' implies a private (possibly face-to-face) setting, not the person's absence.
i.fx: in their absence (behind their back)

i.sp: One should understand that as them knowing good qualities.
i.ev: ཡོན་ཏན་ཤེས་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ: one should recognize the one who speaks of one's qualities as someone who knows good qualities (bo-shenga 5-76 བརྗོད་པ་པོ་དེ། ཡོན་ཏན་ཁོ་ན་ཤེས་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ; bo-gyaltsab 5-76 adds: without arrogance). 'that' and 'them' have no clear referent.
i.fx: one should regard the speaker as one who recognizes good qualities, without becoming conceited.

atts.t:
One should speak of good qualities in their absence,
And if good qualities are spoken of, join in.
If one's own good qualities are spoken of,
One should understand that as them knowing good qualities.

i.sp: One should speak of good qualities in their absence,
i.ev: ལྐོག་ན་ཡོན་ཏན་བརྗོད་བྱ: the qualities are those of others, praised behind their backs to avoid the suspicion of flattery. bo-gyaltsab 5-76: ཁ་གསག་ཏུ་དོགས་པས་ལྐོག་ན་གཞན་གྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ; bo-shenga 5-76 similar. 'Their' has no antecedent in the English.
i.fx: One should speak of others' good qualities behind their backs,

i.sp: One should understand that as them knowing good qualities.
i.ev: ཡོན་ཏན་ཤེས་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ: the one to be recognized as knowing qualities is the speaker who praises one. bo-kunpal 5-76: བརྗོད་མཁན་པོ་དེ ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཤེས་པའི་མཁས་པ ... རིག་པར་བྱ་དགོས; bo-gyaltsab 5-76 adds that one should not become conceited. 'Them' is vague and the sense is hard to parse.
i.fx: one should regard the speaker as someone who recognizes good qualities, and not become conceited.

atts.t:
In this, there is no loss for me here,
And in the next life there is great happiness.
Through faults, there is unhappiness and suffering,
And in the next life there is great suffering.

i.sp: In this, there is no loss for me here,
i.ev: བདག་ལ་འདིར་གོད་ཡོང་མེད་ལ། འདིར = 'here, in this life', contrasted with ཕ་རོལ་དུ (next life); bo-shenga 5-78 ཚེ་འདིར་གོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོང་མེད; bo-kunpal 5-78 ཚེ་འདིར. 'In this ... here' is redundant and leaves 'this' unspecified.
i.fx: In this life there is no loss for me,

atts.t:
In this life there is no loss for me,
And in the next life there is great happiness.
Through faults, there is unhappiness and suffering,
And in the next life there is great suffering.

Whether motivated by constant strong dedication
Or motivated by an antidote,
Toward the fields of good qualities and benefactors,
And those who are suffering, virtue becomes great.

i.sp: strong dedication
i.ev: མངོན་ཞེན་ = intense fixation/zeal; bo-kunpal 5-81 glosses it as འདུན་པ་ཤུགས་དྲག་པོ (powerful aspiration, e.g. from faith and compassion); bo-gyaltsab 5-81 འདུན་པ་དྲག་པོས་བྱ་བ. 'Dedication' suggests dedication of merit (བསྔོ་བ).
i.fx: intense, fixed aspiration

atts.t:
Whether motivated by constant, intense, fixed aspiration,
Or motivated by an antidote,
Toward the fields of good qualities and benefactors,
And those who are suffering, virtue becomes great.

i.sp: constant, intense, fixed aspiration
i.ev: The Tibetan has only རྟག་པར་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱིས་བསླང་བ (motivated constantly / by strong inclination, mngon zhen; Skt sātatyābhiniveśa). bo-kunpal 5-81 glosses མངོན་ཞེན as འདུན་པ་ཤུགས་དྲག་པོ (strong aspiration); nothing corresponds to 'fixed'.
i.fx: motivated by constant, intense aspiration

atts.t:
One should share with those fallen into ruin, the unprotected,
And those established in ascetic discipline;
One should eat only a moderate amount,
And give away everything except the three Dharma robes.

i.sp: those fallen into ruin
i.ev: ལོག་པར་ལྟུང་ = fallen into wrong/lower states; bo-kunpal 5-85 ལོག་པར་ལྟུང་བ་བྱ་ཁྱི་ལ་སོགས་པ་དུད་འགྲོ་; bo-gyaltsab 5-85 adds animals and pretas (དུད་འགྲོ་དང་ཡི་དྭགས). 'Ruin' could be read as worldly (e.g. financial) ruin.
i.fx: those fallen into wretched states (animals and the like)

atts.t:
One should share with those fallen into wretched states, the unprotected,
And those established in ascetic discipline;
One should eat only a moderate amount,
And give away everything except the three Dharma robes.

While the intention of compassion is impure,
One should not give away this body;
By all means, in this and other lives as well,
It should be given as a cause for accomplishing a great purpose.

i.sp: By all means, in this and other lives as well, It should be given as a cause for accomplishing a great purpose.
i.ev: ཅི་ནས་ ... གཏང་ངོ་ is conditional: give the body only when/so that it becomes a cause of great purpose in this and other lives. bo-kunpal 5-87 དོན་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྒྱུར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་དགེ་བའི་བར་ཆད་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་ན་གཏང་ངོ; bo-gyaltsab 5-87 ... རྒྱུར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཚེ་བཏང་ངོ; bo-shenga 5-87 ... རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པར་མཐོང་ན་བཏང་ངོ. 'By all means' reads as an unconditional exhortation to give the body.
i.fx: Rather, only when it becomes a cause for accomplishing a great purpose, in this life and in others, should it be given.

atts.t:
While the intention of compassion is impure,
One should not give away this body;
Rather, only when in this and other lives
It becomes a cause for accomplishing a great purpose, should it be given.

Do not teach the profound and vast to the lesser,
Nor to a woman without a man present;
Toward the lesser and supreme Dharmas,
One should always act with equal respect.

i.sp: to the lesser
i.ev: དམན་ལ་ = to those of lesser capacity/inclination. bo-kunpal 5-89 བློ་དམན་པ་ཉན་རང་གི་ལམ་ལ་མོས་པ; bo-gyaltsab 5-89 བསམ་པ་དམན་པ. The same word 'lesser' then modifies Dharmas in line 3, so the English blurs persons and teachings.
i.fx: to those of lesser capacity

atts.t:
Do not teach the profound and vast to those of lesser capacity,
Nor to a woman without a man present;
Toward the lesser and supreme Dharmas,
One should always act with equal respect.

i.sp: always
i.ev: མཚུངས་པར་གུས་པས་ཀུན་དུ་སྤྱད has ཀུན་དུ་སྤྱད 'engage in / treat fully' (Skt samaṃ gauravam ācaret); there is no word for 'always' (རྟག་ཏུ). bo-gyaltsab 5-89 glosses it ཀུན་ལ་མཚུངས་པར་གུས་པས་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱད་ཅིང་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བར་བྱའོ, with no temporal 'always'.
i.fx: One should treat with equal respect

atts.t:
Those who have become vessels for the vast Dharma
Should not be engaged in the lesser Dharma;
Conduct should not be completely forsaken,
Nor should they be deceived with sūtras and mantras.

i.sp: Nor should they be deceived with sūtras and mantras.
i.ev: མདོ་དང་སྔགས་ཀྱིས་འདྲིད་མི་བྱ་: the agent is the teacher, who should not lure others (into neglecting conduct) with sūtras and mantras. bo-gyaltsab 5-90 མདོ་དང་སྔགས་ཀྱིས་གཞན་འདྲིད་པར་མི་བྱའོ; bo-shenga 5-90 ... ཁྱོད་དག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་འདྲིད་པར་མི་བྱ. The English passive leaves the agent unstated and 'deceived' misses 'lure/entice'.
i.fx: nor should one lure them with sūtras and mantras.

atts.t:
Those who have become vessels for the vast Dharma
Should not be engaged in the lesser Dharma;
Conduct should not be completely forsaken,
Nor should one lure them with sūtras and mantras.

i.sp: wave the arms excessively
i.ev: Tibetan ལག་པ་ཤས་ཆེར་བསྐྱོད་མིན་ཏེ has ལག་པ (hand), not arm; bo-shenga 5-95 and bo-gyaltsab 5-95 likewise speak of hands (ལག་པ), the context being small gestures when handing things over.
i.fx: One should not move the hands excessively

atts.t:
Just as the Protector lay when passing into nirvāṇa,
One should lie down in the desired direction;
With introspection and the thought of rising quickly,
One should firmly apply the mind from the very beginning.

i.sp: With introspection and the thought of rising quickly, One should firmly apply the mind from the very beginning
i.ev: Tibetan ཤེས་བཞིན་མྱུར་དུ་ལྡང་སེམས་ལ། ཐོག་མ་ཉིད་དུ་ངེས་པར་སྦྱར། : ལ marks མྱུར་དུ་ལྡང་སེམས (the thought of rising quickly) as the object to which the mind is applied, and ཤེས་བཞིན is the accompanying introspection. bo-shenga 5-96: མྱུར་དུ་ལྡང་བའི་སེམས་ལ། ཉལ་བའི་ཐོག་མ་ཉིད་དུ་ངེས་པར་སྦྱར་བར་བྱའོ; bo-gyaltsab 5-96: མྱུར་དུ་ལྡང་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པའི་སེམས་ལ་ཐོག་མ་ཉིད་དུ་ངེས་པར་སྦྱར། The English makes the thought of rising a companion of introspection and leaves "apply the mind" without its object.
i.fx: With introspection, one should firmly direct the mind, from the very beginning (of lying down), to the thought of rising quickly

atts.t:
Just as the Protector lay when passing into nirvāṇa,
One should lie down in the desired direction;
With introspection, to the thought of rising quickly,
One should firmly direct the mind from the very beginning.

Although the conduct of the bodhisattva for awakening
Is taught to be measureless,
One should certainly practice
The conduct of purifying the mind for that long.

i.sp: the bodhisattva for awakening
i.ev: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྤྱོད་པ་ is rendered with the locked "conduct of the bodhisattva"; བྱང་ཆུབ་ is part of the word བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ (bodhisattva), and no separate "for awakening" is in the Tibetan.
i.fx: Although the conduct of bodhisattvas

i.sp: for that long
i.ev: དེ་སྲིད་ is correlative: bo-shenga 5-97 specifies the span as ངེས་པར་བློ་མ་འབྱུང་གི་བར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ and bo-gyaltsab 5-97 as ངེས་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ནུས་པ་དེ་སྲིད་, i.e. until one is able to practice all of it. "For that long" has no antecedent in the English.
i.fx: for as long as one is unable to practice it all (until one can do so)

atts.t:
Although the conduct of bodhisattvas
Is taught to be measureless,
One should certainly practice
The conduct of purifying the mind until one is able to practice it all.

i.sp: until one is able to practice it all
i.ev: The Tibetan says only དེ་སྲིད་ 'for that long / so long' with no stated end-point. The commentaries differ: bo-gyaltsab 5-97 reads ངེས་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ནུས་པ་དེ་སྲིད་ (until able to practise all), while bo-kunpal 5-97 reads སེམས་སྦྱོང་མ་ཐུབ་པར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ (so long as the mind has not been trained). The English commits to one commentary's reading.
i.fx: One should certainly practice the conduct of purifying the mind for that long.

atts.t:
Three times by day and three times by night,
One should recite the Three Heaps Sūtra;
By relying on the Victor and the bodhicitta of awakening,
One should thereby pacify the remaining downfalls.

i.sp: the bodhicitta of awakening
i.ev: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་ is locked as "bodhicitta"; "of awakening" duplicates the བྱང་ཆུབ་ already contained in the term (bo-shenga 5-98: རང་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས).
i.fx: the Victor and bodhicitta

atts.t:
Three times by day and three times by night,
One should recite the Three Heaps Sūtra;
By relying on the Victors and bodhicitta,
One should thereby pacify the remaining downfalls.

That which is not a training for the children of the Victors
Does not exist at all;
For the wise who abide in this way,
There is nothing that does not become merit.

i.sp: That which is not a training for the children of the Victors Does not exist at all
i.ev: Tibetan རྒྱལ་སྲས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མི་བསླབ་པ། དེ་ནི་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་མིན: the agent is the Victors' children (ཀྱིས) and the verb is བསླབ (train in): nothing exists that they do not train in. Sanskrit yan na śikṣyaṃ jinātmajaiḥ; bo-shenga 5-100: རིག་པའི་གནས་ཀུན་ལ་མི་བསླབ་པ། དེ་ནི་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མིན.
i.fx: There is nothing at all that the children of the Victors do not train in

atts.t:
That which is not a training for the children of the Victors
Does not exist at all;
For the wise who abide in this way,
There is nothing that does not become merit.

Always, a spiritual friend
Who is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna
And the supreme ascetic discipline of the bodhisattvas of awakening,
Should not be given up even for the sake of one's life.

i.sp: Who is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna And the supreme ascetic discipline of the bodhisattvas of awakening
i.ev: The spiritual friend is learned only in the Mahāyāna meaning (ཐེག་ཆེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ); the བརྟུལ་ཞུགས་མཆོག is what the friend holds or abides in. bo-kunpal 5-102: སྤྱོད་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སམ་བརྟུལ་ཞུགས་མཆོག་སྟེ་སྡོམ་པ་ལ་གནས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན; Sanskrit bodhisattvavratadharaṃ mahāyānārthakovidam. The English makes the discipline a second object of learning.
i.fx: Who is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna and who keeps the supreme ascetic discipline of the bodhisattvas

i.sp: bodhisattvas of awakening
i.ev: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ is the single locked term "bodhisattva"; "of awakening" is not in the Tibetan.
i.fx: the bodhisattvas

atts.t:
Always, a spiritual friend
Who is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna
And who keeps the supreme ascetic discipline of the bodhisattvas,
Should not be given up even for the sake of one's life.
From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the fifth chapter: guarding introspection for a bodhisattva's awakening.

i.sp: guarding introspection for a bodhisattva's awakening
i.ev: Tibetan ཤེས་བཞིན་བསྲུང་བར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལེའུ་ལྔ་པའོ: the chapter is titled "Guarding Introspection"; བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ is already used in the work title བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པ་ལས. The phrase "for a bodhisattva's awakening" has no counterpart and misreads the title.
i.fx: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the fifth chapter: Guarding Introspection.

atts.t: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the fifth chapter: Guarding Introspection.

terms: Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva

atts.t:
There is no misdeed like hatred;
There is no austerity like patience.
Therefore, earnestly upon patience,
One should practice meditation in various ways.

i.sp:
Therefore, earnestly upon patience,
One should practice meditation in various ways.
i.ev: བཟོད་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ། སྣ་ཚོགས་ཚུལ་དུ་བསྒོམ་པར་བྱ། ("meditate on patience earnestly in various ways"; bo-kunpal 6-2: བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ). The English splits "patience" from the verb "practice meditation", leaving "earnestly upon patience" a dangling phrase that is hard to parse.
i.fx: Therefore, one should earnestly meditate on patience in various ways.

atts.t:
There is no misdeed like hatred;
There is no austerity like patience.
Therefore, earnestly regarding patience,
One should practice meditation in various ways.

i.sp: earnestly regarding patience, One should practice meditation in various ways
i.ev: བཟོད་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ། སྣ་ཚོགས་ཚུལ་དུ་བསྒོམ་པར་བྱ: བཟོད་ལ་ is the object of བསྒོམ ('meditate on / cultivate patience', Skt kṣāntiṃ bhāvayet; bo-gyaltsab 6-2 བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ). 'Regarding patience, practice meditation' loosens the object relation and is awkward.
i.fx: Therefore one should earnestly cultivate meditation on patience in various ways.

atts.t:
The enemy of anger produces
These and other such sufferings.
Whoever strives to destroy anger
Is happy in this life and the next.

i.sp: The enemy of anger produces
i.ev: ཁྲོ་བའི་དགྲ་ཡིས་ is appositional: anger is itself the enemy that produces these sufferings (Sanskrit: karoti ity arisaṃjñayā; bo-kunpal 6-6: ཁྲོ་བའི་དགྲ་ཡིས་དགེ་རྩ་འཇོམས་ཤིང་དམྱལ་བར་སྐྱེ་བ་སོགས་...སྡུག་བསྔལ་མང་པོ་དག་ནི་ཕྱེད་པར་འགྱུར; bo-shenga 6-6: ཁྲོ་བའི་དགྲ་ཡིས་དེ་དག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་...སྡུག་བསྔལ་དག་ནི་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར). "Enemy of anger" would mean someone opposed to anger, reversing the agent.
i.fx: The enemy, anger, produces

atts.t:
The enemy, anger, produces
These and other such sufferings.
Whoever strives to destroy anger
Is happy in this life and the next.

i.sp: Whoever strives to destroy anger
i.ev: Tibetan གང་ཞིག་བསྒྲིམས་ཏེ་ཁྲོ་འཇོམས་པ states that the person (resolutely) destroys anger; Sanskrit 'yaḥ krodhaṃ hanti nirbandhāt'. Kunpal 6-6 glosses ཁྲོ་བའི་དགྲ་དེ་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ. 'Strives to' turns an accomplished act into mere attempt and loses བསྒྲིམས་ཏེ ('firmly/determinedly').
i.fx: Whoever resolutely destroys anger

atts.t:
For myself or for my friends,
Suffering, contempt, harsh words,
And disrepute are not desired;
For an enemy, it is the opposite.

i.sp: For an enemy, it is the opposite.
i.ev: དགྲ་ལ་དེ་ལས་བཟློག་པས་སོ། ends with the reason particle པས་སོ ("because for an enemy it is the reverse of that"); bo-gyaltsab 6-11 ties the reversal of wanting/not-wanting to the enemy as the reason. The English drops the causal link and leaves "it" vague.
i.fx: because, for an enemy, these are the reverse (what is wanted rather than unwanted).

atts.t:
For myself or for my friends,
Suffering, contempt, harsh words,
And disrepute are not desired,
Because for an enemy it is the reverse.

Devotees of Durgā and the Karṇapas
Endure the feeling of burning, cutting, and so forth
Pointlessly; for the sake of liberation,
Why then am I cowardly?

i.sp: Why then am I cowardly?
i.ev: བདག་གོ་ཅི་ཕྱིར་སྔར། has no word for "coward" (the Sanskrit kātaraḥ does). bo-kunpal 6-13 glosses it as "why is it not fitting for me to endure" (ཅི་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་སྔར་ཏེ་སྔར་མི་རིགས་སོ), and bo-gyaltsab 6-13 as "why should I not endure it" (བདག་ཀོ་ཅི་ཞིག་བསྟར་ཏེ་བཟོད་པར་རིགས་སོ).
i.fx: why should I not endure it?

atts.t:
Devotees of Durgā and the Karṇapas
Endure the feeling of burning, cutting, and so forth
Pointlessly; for the sake of liberation,
Why should I not endure it?

Furthermore, the good quality of suffering is:
Through sorrow, haughtiness is dispelled,
Compassion arises for those in saṃsāra,
One shuns misdeeds and delights in virtue.

i.sp: Through sorrow
i.ev: སྐྱོ་བས is weariness or disenchantment with saṃsāra (Sanskrit saṃvega), not grief: bo-shenga 6-21 སེམས་སྐྱོ་བར་གྱུར་པས; bo-kunpal 6-21 ཡིད་འབྱུང་ཞིང་སྐྱོ་བར་གྱུར་པས ("becoming weary, disenchanted"). "Sorrow" suggests grief.
i.fx: Through disillusionment (weariness with saṃsāra)

atts.t:
Furthermore, the good quality of suffering is:
Through disillusionment, haughtiness is dispelled,
Compassion arises for those in saṃsāra,
One shuns misdeeds and delights in virtue.

Even without thinking, "I shall become angry,"
People become angry spontaneously;
Even without thinking, "I shall produce it,"
Anger likewise arises.

i.sp: People become angry spontaneously
i.ev: སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ནི་གྱི་ནར་ཁྲོ། (gyi nar = on whatever slight condition happens along). bo-kunpal 6-24: 'རྐྱེན་ཕལ་པ་ཙམ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཁྲོ་བར་འགྱུར' (becomes angry depending on a mere ordinary condition); bo-shenga 6-24: 'རྐྱེན་ཇི་ནར་ཙམ་གྱིས'. 'Spontaneously' can read as uncaused, which the passage's argument (all arises from conditions) excludes.
i.fx: People become angry at the slightest condition

atts.t:
Even without thinking, "I shall become angry,"
People become angry at the slightest condition;
Even without thinking, "I shall produce it,"
Anger likewise arises.

If, even at the time of acting, it remains as before,
What has the action done to it?
In saying, "This is its action,"
What connection could there be?

i.sp: In saying, "This is its action," What connection could there be?
i.ev: དེ་ཡི་བྱེད་པ་འདི་ཡིན་ཞེས། འབྲེལ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཞིག་ཡོད། asks what relation exists by which one could say 'this is its action'; bo-gyaltsab 6-30: 'བདག་དེའི་... བྱེད་པ་འདི་ཡིན་ཞེས་བདག་དང་འབྲེལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཞིག་ཡོད'. 'In saying' wrongly suggests the connection lies in the act of saying.
i.fx: What connection could there be by which one could say, "This is its action"?

atts.t:
If, even at the time of acting, it remains as before,
What has the action done to it?
What connection could there be
By which one could say, "This is its action"?

Thus, everything is under the power of others,
And through that power, it is powerless.
Knowing this, one will not become angry
At any entities, which are like emanations.

i.sp: which are like emanations
i.ev: The Tibetan as given reads སྦྲུལ་ལྟ་བུའི ('snake-like'), also in bo-shenga 6-31 (སྦྲུལ་ལྟ་བུའི་རང་བཞིན), whereas the Sanskrit has nirmāṇavat and bo-kunpal/bo-gyaltsab 6-31 read སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ / སྤྲུལ་ལྟ་བུ (emanation). The English follows the Sanskrit and commentaries, not the Tibetan wording; the divergence should be flagged for the reader.
i.fx: which are like emanations [the Tibetan text here reads sbrul, 'snake', likely a scribal error for sprul]

atts.t:
Thus, everything is under the power of others,
And through that power, it is powerless.
Knowing this, one will not become angry
At any entities, which are like emanations.

Through heedlessness, they even harm themselves
With thorns and so forth;
In order to obtain women and the like,
They become obsessed and engage in fasting and so forth.

i.sp: they become obsessed
i.ev: རྔམ་ཞིང (vehement, fierce, in a fervor). Sanskrit has kopāt ('out of anger'); bo-gyaltsab 6-35 'རྔམ་ཞིང་ཁྲོས་པས' (fierce and angry), bo-kunpal 'རྔམ་ཞིང་ཆགས་ནས', bo-shenga 'བརྣབ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་རྔམ་ཞིང'. 'Obsessed' loses the sense of fierce vehemence/anger.
i.fx: they grow vehement (in fury)

atts.t:
Through heedlessness, they even harm themselves
With thorns and so forth;
In order to obtain women and the like,
They grow vehement and engage in fasting and so forth.

When, through the arising of afflictions,
They engage in such acts as killing themselves,
If compassion does not even arise,
What point is there in feeling anger?

i.sp: When, through the arising of afflictions, They engage in such acts as killing themselves, If compassion does not even arise,
i.ev: བདག་གསོད་ལ་སོགས་ཞུགས་པ་ལ། སྙིང་རྗེ་རྒྱ་ལ་མ་སྐྱེས་ན། — compassion fails to arise toward ('ལ') those who engage in self-harm (bo-gyaltsab 6-38: 'བདག་གསོད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བར་འོས'). The English 'When ... they engage' leaves the object of compassion unstated and parses as two unrelated clauses.
i.fx: For those who, through the arising of afflictions, engage in such acts as killing themselves, if compassion does not even arise [toward them], what sense is there in anger?

atts.t:
For those who, through the arising of afflictions,
Engage in such acts as killing themselves,
If compassion does not even arise,
What sense is there in anger?

While sticks and the like are directly employed,
If I feel anger toward the one who wields them,
Since they too are impelled by hatred,
If anything, it is appropriate to feel anger at hatred.

i.sp: If I feel anger
i.ev: གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པ་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན། has no first-person subject; bo-gyaltsab 6-41 treats it as impersonal ('གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན'). The Sanskrit has kupyate (passive/impersonal).
i.fx: if one feels anger

i.sp: While sticks and the like are directly employed,
i.ev: དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་དངོས་བཀོལ་ཏེ། — sticks etc. are the actual instruments (dngos) the person employs; bo-shenga 6-41: 'དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་བཀོལ་ཏེ་ལུས་ལ་བརྡེག་པ་ན' (having employed sticks etc., when they strike the body). 'While ... directly employed' is a confusing temporal/concessive rendering. Also 'ཉིས་ན' (bo-shenga: 'གཅིག་ཏུ... ཉེས་ན་སྟེ་གཉིས་སུ་ན', 'firstly the sticks; secondly, hatred') is rendered as 'If anything'.
i.fx: Having employed sticks and the like as the actual instruments, if one is angry at the one who throws them, since he too is driven by hatred, then, in the second place, it is fitting to be angry at hatred.

atts.t:
Having employed sticks and the like as the actual instruments,
if one feels anger at the one who throws them,
since he too is driven by hatred,
then, in the second place, it is fitting to feel anger at hatred.

i.sp: Having employed sticks and the like as the actual instruments, if one feels anger at the one who throws them
i.ev: དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་དངོས་བཀོལ་ཏེ། གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པ་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན། The one who employs (བཀོལ) the sticks is the thrower (bo-shenga 6-41: 'དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་བཀོལ་ཏེ་ལུས་ལ་བརྡེག་པ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པ་པོ་ཉིད་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན'; bo-kunpal 6-41). In the English the participle 'Having employed' has the grammatical subject 'one' (the angry victim), so it reads as if the victim employed the sticks.
i.fx: Since he employs sticks and the like as the actual instruments, if one feels anger at the one who throws them,

atts.t:
His weapon and my body,
Both are causes of suffering;
Since he produced the weapon and I the body,
At whom should I direct my anger?

i.sp: Since he produced the weapon and I the body
i.ev: Tibetan ཕྱུང་ (དེས་མཚོན་བདག་གི་ལུས་ཕྱུང་ན) means drew out/brought forth; bo-shenga 6-43 glosses "དགྲ་བོ་དེས་མཚོན་ཕྱུང་ཞིང་བདག་གིས་ལུས་ཕྱུང་ན", bo-kunpal "མཚོན་ཆ་ཕྱུངས་ཤིང་... ལུས་ཕྱུང་ནས". Sanskrit gṛhīta "taken up". "Produced" implies creation, not drawing out/taking up.
i.fx: Since he has drawn the weapon and I have taken up the body,

atts.t:
His weapon and my body,
both are causes of suffering;
since he has drawn the weapon and I have taken up the body,
at whom should I direct my anger?

Childish ones do not desire suffering,
Yet they crave the causes of suffering;
When harmed by their own faults,
Why should they resent others?

i.sp: Why should they resent others?
i.ev: Tibetan གཞན་ལ་བཀོན་དུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད། — བཀོན་ is "to blame/lay the fault on" (bo-kunpal: "གཞན་ལ་ཁྲོ་ཞིང་བཀོན་དུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད"; bo-shenga "གཞན་དགྲ་བོ་དག་ལ་བཀོན་ཏུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད"), not inner resentment; also the Tibetan is "what is there to blame on others", a statement of there being no basis.
i.fx: what grounds are there to blame others?

atts.t:
Childish ones do not desire suffering,
yet they crave the causes of suffering;
when harmed by their own faults,
what grounds are there to blame others?

Impelled by my own karma,
Those who harm me appear;
If by this they go to the hell of sentient beings,
Have I not ruined them?

i.sp: If by this they go to the hell of sentient beings,
i.ev: Tibetan སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་འདོང་ན is "if beings (the enemies) go to hell": སེམས་ཅན is the subject, དམྱལ(་བར) the destination. Not a hell called "of sentient beings". Sanskrit "yena yāsyanti narakāt" and bo-shenga 6-47 "དགྲ་དེ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བར་འདོང་ན", bo-gyaltsab "གང་ཟག་དེ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བར་འདོར་བར་འགྱུར་ན" confirm the enemies go to hell. The locked-term entry སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ is a mis-segmentation.
i.fx: If because of this those beings go to hell,

atts.t:
Impelled by my own karma,
Those who harm me appear;
If because of this those beings go to hell,
Have I not ruined them?

To embodied beings, beings with a mind
And the insentient both cause harm;
Why single out beings with a mind for resentment?
Therefore, practice patience toward harm.

i.sp:
To embodied beings, beings with a mind
And the insentient both cause harm;
i.ev: ལུས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སེམས་ཡོད་དང་། སེམས་མེད་གཉི་གས་གནོད་བྱས་ན། — 'embodied beings' are the recipients of harm; 'sentient' (སེམས་ཡོད) and 'insentient' (སེམས་མེད) are the two agents (bo-shenga 6-66: སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སེམས་ཡོད་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་དང་སེམས་མེད་པའི་ནད་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཉིས་ཀས་གནོད་པར་བྱས་ན). The English comma lets 'beings with a mind' read in apposition to 'embodied beings'.
i.fx:
If both beings with a mind
and the insentient cause harm to embodied beings;

atts.t:
If both beings with a mind
and the insentient cause harm to embodied beings,
why single out beings with a mind to blame?
Therefore, practice patience toward harm.

Likewise, whatever the mind has attachment to,
Causing the fire of hatred to spread,
Out of fear that merit will be burned,
That must be discarded instantly.

i.sp:
whatever the mind has attachment to,
Causing the fire of hatred to spread,
i.ev: གང་ལ་སེམས་ཆགས་ནས། ཞེ་སྡང་མེ་ནི་མཆེད་གྱུར་པ། — the fire of hatred has spread (intransitive, མཆེད་གྱུར་པ) onto the object of attachment (bo-gyaltsab 6-71: ཆགས་པའི་གཞི་དེ་ནི...). The dangling participle 'Causing' obscures what causes what.
i.fx: whatever the mind is attached to, in which the fire of hatred has spread,

atts.t:
Likewise, whatever the mind has attachment to,
In which the fire of hatred has spread,
Out of fear that merit will be burned,
That must be discarded instantly.

Thinking, "In that way, the other will be happy,"
If you do not desire this happiness,
Through forsaking the giving of wages and the like,
The seen and unseen will be ruined.

i.ev: The line begins གཞན་ཡང་དེ་ལྟར་བདེ་འགྱུར་ཞེས། ('Moreover / Furthermore'); the English drops གཞན་ཡང་, which marks this as a further argument (bo-gyaltsab 6-78 repeats གཞན་ཡང་).
i.fx: Moreover, thinking, "In that way, the other will be happy,"

atts.t:
Moreover, thinking, "In that way, the other will be happy,"
If you do not desire this happiness,
Through forsaking the giving of wages and the like,
The seen and unseen will be ruined.

Whoever is a dependent you nurture,
To whom you yourself must give,
If those relatives find a livelihood,
Will you not be glad, but instead become angry?

i.sp: Will you not be glad, but instead become angry?
i.ev: དགར་མི་འགྱུར་བར་སླར་ཁྲོའམ། is "instead of being glad, do you (rather) get angry?" (bo-shenga 6-82: དགའ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བར་སླར་དེ་ལ་ཁྲོའམ་ཅི། ; Skt na hṛṣyasi prakupyasi). The English "Will you not be glad" can be read as asking whether you will be glad.
i.fx: Instead of being glad, do you become angry in return?

atts.t:
Whoever is a dependent you nurture,
To whom you yourself must give,
If those relatives find a livelihood,
Instead of being glad, do you become angry in return?

Merit and faith,
Or your own good qualities, why do you cast them away?
Not taking hold of the gains that occur,
Tell me, why do you not become angry?

i.sp: Not taking hold of the gains that occur,
i.ev: རྙེད་པ་གྱུར་པ་མི་འཛིན་པ། is explained as not holding the causes that bring gain (bo-kunpal 6-85: རྙེད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་པ་ཡི་རྒྱུ་དེ་དག་མི་འཛིན་པ; bo-gyaltsab: རྙེད་པ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྒྱུ་མི་འཛིན་པ). The English reads as failing to take gains already received; also the object of the anger (oneself) is left unstated (bo-gyaltsab: ཁྲོ་ན་རང་ཉིད་ལ་ཁྲོ་བར་རིགས་སོ།).
i.fx: Not holding on to what would bring you gains, tell me, why are you not angry at yourself?

atts.t:
Merit and faith,
Or your own good qualities, why do you cast them away?
Not holding on to what would bring you gains,
Tell me, why are you not angry at yourself?

Cast by the fisherman of the afflictions,
This hook is an unbearable barb;
Caught by it, in the cauldrons of hell,
The hell guardians will certainly boil me.

i.sp: an unbearable barb
i.ev: མི་བཟད་གཟེ། means unbearable and fierce/terrible (bo-kunpal: གཟེ་བའམ་རྣོ་བ; bo-shenga: འཇིགས་པའི་གནས་ཡིན་པས་མི་བཟད་པར་གཟེ་བ; Skt ghora). "Barb" is not what གཟེ conveys and "hook ... barb" is redundant.
i.fx: is unbearable and terrible

atts.t:
Cast by the fisherman of the afflictions,
This hook is unbearable and terrible;
Caught by it, in the cauldrons of hell,
The hell guardians will certainly boil me.

First of all, since sound is mindless,
It cannot possibly have the intention to praise me.
As for the renown that "Others are pleased with me,"
Perhaps that is the cause of joy?

i.sp: the renown that "Others are pleased with me,"
i.ev: བདག་ལ་གཞན་དགའ་ཞེས་གྲགས་པ། here grags pa is "being said/known" that another is pleased (bo-shenga 6-94: བདག་ལ་གཞན་བསྟོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དགའ་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་གྲགས་པ), not "renown" in the sense of fame (the glossary sense of གྲགས་པ).
i.fx: the fact that it is said, "Others are pleased with me,"

atts.t:
First of all, since sound is mindless,
It cannot possibly have the intention to praise me.
As for the fact that it is said, "Others are pleased with me,"
Perhaps that is the cause of joy?

If you say that because they lack the intention to accomplish patience,
This enemy is not to be venerated,
Since it is a fit cause for accomplishment,
Why do you venerate the sublime Dharma?

i.sp:
Since it is a fit cause for accomplishment,
Why do you venerate the sublime Dharma?
i.ev: Tibetan གྲུབ་པ་ཡི་ནི་རྒྱུར་རུང་བ། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་སྟེ་མཆོད། means 'why do you venerate even the sublime Dharma, which is a fit cause of accomplishment [yet lacks the intention]'; ཀྱང 'even' is dropped and the Dharma is not made the subject of the clause. Sanskrit siddhihetur acitto 'pi saddharmaḥ pūjyate katham ('though without intention'). Kunpal 6-109 and Gyaltsab 6-109: the Dharma likewise lacks the thought 'I will generate virtue' (དགེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པའི་བསམ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར), so the opponent's reason would wrongly make it unworthy of veneration too. English 'Since it is a fit cause' with an unresolved 'it' reads as a reason for venerating the enemy and loses the parallel.
i.fx: Why then do you venerate even the sublime Dharma, which, though a fit cause for accomplishment, has no such intention?

atts.t:
If you say that because he lacks the intention to accomplish patience,
This enemy is not to be venerated,
Why do you venerate even the sublime Dharma,
Which is a fit cause for accomplishment?

It is not by the good quality of intention itself,
But it is from the result that they are similar.
Sentient beings too possess good qualities,
And therefore they are equal.

i.sp:
But it is from the result that they are similar.
Sentient beings too possess good qualities,
i.ev: Tibetan འབྲས་བུ་ལས་ཡིན་དེས་མཚུངས་པར། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལའང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡོད། has དེས་མཚུངས་པར 'just as [the Buddhas]' (Kunpal 6-114: སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་དང་མཚུངས་པར་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལའང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡོད), which the English drops; 'they' in line 2 has no stated referent (Buddhas and sentient beings, as fields; Gyaltsab 6-114).
i.fx: But it is from the result that [the two] are alike. Just like the Buddhas, sentient beings too possess good qualities,

atts.t:
It is not by the good quality of intention itself,
But it is from the result that the two are alike.
Just like the Buddhas, sentient beings too possess good qualities,
And therefore they are equal.

Because they have a share in accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha,
They are therefore asserted to be equal.
Yet to those with an infinite ocean of good qualities,
To the Buddhas, no one is equal.

i.sp: They are therefore asserted to be equal.
i.ev: Tibetan དེས་ན་དེ་དག་མཉམ་པར་འདོད 'therefore those two [sentient beings and Buddhas] are held to be equal'. Kunpal 6-116: སེམས་ཅན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་དེ་དག་མཉམ་པར་འདོད; Sanskrit sattvā jinaiḥ samāḥ. English 'They' has no stated counterpart, so the equality is not tied to sentient beings and the Buddhas.
i.fx: Therefore sentient beings and the Buddhas are held to be equal.

atts.t:
Because they have a share in accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha,
Therefore sentient beings and the Buddhas are held to be equal.
Yet to those with an infinite ocean of good qualities,
To the Buddhas, no one is equal.

i.sp:
Yet to those with an infinite ocean of good qualities,
To the Buddhas, no one is equal.
i.ev: Lines 3-4 are one clause: ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱ་མཚོ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི། སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་དང་འགའ་མི་མཉམ། "none is equal to the Buddhas, who have an infinite ocean of qualities" (bo-shenga 6-116: ...རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་དང་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོན་ཏན་མི་མཉམ་མོ). The English splits it into a dangling "to those ... / To the Buddhas" with "to" for དང་, which is garbled.
i.fx:
Yet none are equal to the Buddhas,
who have an infinite ocean of good qualities.

atts.t:
