i.fx: For the sake of living beings alone, I should share all the goodness for awakening.

atts.t: Whether directly or indirectly, I should only do things that help living beings. For the sake of living beings alone, I should give everything to awakening by sharing the goodness.
I should learn how to rely on a teacher from the life story of Shrisambhava. I will know this and other things spoken by the Buddha by reading the scriptures.

i.sp: I will know this and other things spoken by the Buddha by reading the scriptures.
i.ev: These and other words spoken by the Buddha should be known by reading the sutras (an instruction, not a prediction).
i.fx: I should read the scriptures to learn this and other things the Buddha taught.

atts.t: I should learn how to rely on a teacher from the life story of Shrisambhava. I should read the scriptures to learn this and other things the Buddha taught.
The enemy of anger produces these and other kinds of suffering. Whoever tries hard to destroy anger will be happy in this life and the next.

i.sp: The enemy of anger produces these and other kinds of suffering.
i.ev: "The enemy, anger, produces these and other such sufferings": anger itself is the enemy that causes suffering, not an enemy of anger.
i.fx: Anger is an enemy, and it brings these and other kinds of suffering.

atts.t: Anger is an enemy, and it brings these and other kinds of suffering. Whoever tries hard to destroy anger will be happy in this life and the next.
Think of snakes and biting flies. Think of the feeling of hunger and thirst. Think of itchy rashes. Why do you not see that all this suffering is pointless?

i.sp: Why do you not see that all this suffering is pointless?
i.ev: Why do you not see their pointless suffering? The suffering of those afflicted by snakes, flies, hunger, thirst and rashes is the pointless kind; it does not say all suffering is pointless (cf. 6-21).
i.fx: Those who suffer from snakes, biting flies, hunger, thirst and rashes suffer for no purpose. Why do you not see this?

atts.t: Think of snakes, biting flies, itchy rashes, and the feeling of hunger and thirst. The suffering they bring is pointless. Why do you not see this?
Even when suffering happens, wise people keep a clear mind. They are fighting a war against troubling emotions. Many harms happen during a battle.

i.ev: "for in waging war against the afflictions, harms are many": the war is the reason the wise should not cloud the mind.
i.fx: Even when suffering happens, wise people keep a clear mind. This is because they are fighting a war against troubling emotions, and many harms happen during a battle.

atts.t: Even when suffering happens, wise people keep a clear mind. This is because they are fighting a war against troubling emotions, and many harms happen during a battle.
Suffering also has a good quality. Sadness stops us from feeling superior. We feel compassion for those in the cycle of rebirth. We avoid harmful deeds and enjoy good deeds.

i.sp: Sadness stops us from feeling superior.
i.ev: Through disillusionment (weariness with suffering), haughtiness is dispelled; not mere sadness.
i.fx: Getting tired of suffering stops us from feeling superior.

atts.t: Suffering also has a good quality. Getting tired of suffering stops us from feeling superior. We feel compassion for those in the cycle of rebirth. We avoid harmful deeds and enjoy good deeds.
So, everything is controlled by other forces. Because of this power, everything is powerless. Knowing this, I will not get angry at any things. They are just like magic illusions.

i.sp: I will not get angry at any things
i.ev: Academic: 'Knowing this, one will not become angry at any entities' - a general consequence, not a personal vow.
i.fx: Knowing this, a person will not get angry at any things.

i.sp: magic illusions
i.ev: Academic: 'entities, which are like emanations' (sprul pa) - something conjured up, not an illusion.
i.fx: They are like things that magic has conjured up.

atts.t: Everything is controlled by other forces. Because of this power, everything is powerless. Knowing this, a person will not get angry at any things. They are like things that magic has conjured up.
Someone might ask, "What can stop what? Even stopping things makes no sense!" But because things depend on each other, it does make sense. It is not wrong to wish for sufferings to be cut away.

i.sp: because things depend on each other
i.ev: Academic: 'In dependence upon that' - i.e. on conditions/causes, not mutual dependence.
i.fx: But because suffering depends on its causes, it does make sense.

atts.t: Someone might ask, "What can stop what? Even stopping things makes no sense!" But because suffering depends on its causes, it does make sense. It is not wrong to wish for suffering to be cut away.

i.sp: because suffering depends on its causes
i.ev: Academic: 'In dependence upon that, it is not unreasonable to wish for sufferings to be severed'; 'that' is not specified as suffering's causes.
i.fx: But because things depend on each other, it does make sense. It is not wrong to wish for suffering to be cut away.

atts.t: Therefore, whether it is an enemy or a friend, if I see them doing something wrong, I will think, "This has come from these circumstances." I will think this way and stay at ease.

i.sp: I will think ... I will think this way and stay at ease
i.ev: Academic: imperative advice, 'Reflect in this way and remain at ease', not a personal resolution.
i.fx: think, "This has come from these circumstances." Think this way and stay at ease.

atts.t: Therefore, if you see an enemy or a friend doing something wrong, think, "This has come from these circumstances." Think this way and stay at ease.
Someone might hit me with a stick. If I feel anger at the person swinging it, I must remember they are driven by hatred. It makes more sense to feel anger at hatred itself.

i.sp: I must remember they are driven by hatred
i.ev: Academic: 'since he too is driven by hatred, then in the second place it is fitting to feel anger at hatred' - a reason, not an instruction to remember.
i.fx: If I feel anger at the person swinging it, remember he is driven by hatred too. So the anger really belongs to the hatred.

atts.t: Someone might hit me with a stick. If I feel anger at the person swinging it, since he is driven by hatred too, it makes more sense to feel anger at hatred.

i.sp: since he is driven by hatred too
i.ev: Academic: sticks are the actual instruments, and the thrower too is driven by hatred, so anger at hatred is the fitting target; 'too' has no referent in the children's text, and the stick-as-tool point is lost.
i.fx: Someone hits me with a stick. I do not blame the stick, because the person swinging it is pushing it. But that person is pushed by hatred too. So it makes more sense to be angry at hatred.

atts.t: If my intention has a good quality, I will not go to hell. But if I just protect myself, what will happen to them?

i.sp: But if I just protect myself
i.ev: Academic: 'If I protect myself, what will happen to them here?' - no contrast ('But') and no 'just'; 'here' also dropped.
i.fx: If my intention has a good quality, I will not go to hell. If I protect myself, what will happen to them here?

atts.t: If my intention has a good quality, I will not go to hell. If I protect myself, what will happen to them here?
In the same way, the fire of hatred spreads to whatever the mind has clinging to. To stop my store of goodness from burning, I must throw that clinging away right now.

i.sp: I must throw that clinging away right now
i.ev: The thing to be discarded is whatever the mind clings to (the object, like the straw the fire has caught on), not the clinging itself.
i.fx: To stop my store of goodness from burning, I must throw away right now whatever my mind is clinging to.

atts.t: In the same way, the fire of hatred spreads to whatever the mind is clinging to. To stop my store of goodness from burning, I must throw away right now whatever my mind is clinging to.
You feel no sorrow for the harmful deeds you yourself have done. On top of that, do you want to compete with others who have built up a store of goodness? The Second Fascicle.

i.sp: The Second Fascicle.
i.ev: This is the colophon marking the end of a section of the manuscript, not part of the verse; 'fascicle' is a hard unexplained word for ages 8-12.
i.fx: Drop it or say: 'This is the end of the second part of the book.'

atts.t: You feel no sorrow for the harmful deeds you yourself have done. On top of that, do you want to compete with others who have built up a store of goodness? This is the end of the second part of the book.
If I really knew my own good, what own good is there in that? If I only want my mind to feel happy, I must also rely on gambling and alcohol.

i.sp: If I really knew my own good, what own good is there in that?
i.ev: Academic: 'If I were to know my own welfare, what welfare of mine is there in that?' (in praise and fame); also drops 'and the like' after gambling and alcohol.
i.fx: Even if I knew what is truly good for me, what good would praise do me? If I only want my mind to feel happy, I would also have to turn to gambling, alcohol, and things like that.

atts.t: Even if I knew my own good, what own good is there in that? If I only want my mind to feel happy, I would also have to turn to gambling, alcohol, and things like that.
Some people are around just to destroy my praise. Are they not protecting me from falling into an unhappy realm?

i.sp: destroy my praise
i.ev: 'my praise and so forth' - the list of such things (fame, honor) is dropped.
i.fx: Some people are around to destroy my praise and things like it. Are they not protecting me from falling into an unhappy realm?

atts.t: Therefore, some people are around to destroy my praise and things like it. Are they not protecting me from falling into an unhappy realm?
If my own faults stop me from practicing patience with this, I am the one making a block. The cause of a store of goodness is right in front of me.

i.sp: I am the one making a block.
i.ev: The academic text says I am creating an obstacle to the cause of merit that is present; the children's text does not say what the block blocks.
i.fx: If my own faults stop me from being patient with this, I am only blocking my own store of goodness, even though its cause is right in front of me.

atts.t: If my own faults stop me from practicing patience with this, I am only making a block, even when the cause of a store of goodness is right in front of me.

i.sp: I am only making a block, even when the cause of a store of goodness is right in front of me
i.ev: Academic: when the cause of merit is present, I am merely creating an obstacle to it (the obstacle is to the cause of merit); 'even when' also shifts the logic.
i.fx: If my own faults stop me from practicing patience with this, I am only blocking the cause of a store of goodness that is right here.

terms: cause of a store of goodness

atts.t: A beggar arriving at the right time is not a block to giving. Someone who helps you in becoming a monk or nun cannot be called a block to becoming a monk or nun.

i.sp: Someone who helps you in becoming a monk or nun
i.ev: The academic text says one who grants ordination (the one who makes someone go forth), not just anyone who helps.
i.fx: Someone who gives you the vows of a monk or nun cannot be called a block to becoming a monk or nun.

atts.t: A beggar who arrives at the right time is not a block to giving. Someone who gives you the vows of a monk or nun cannot be called a block to becoming a monk or nun.
Therefore, patience only arises because of a very hateful mind. Since they are the exact cause of patience, they deserve to be honored just like the holy teachings.

i.sp: patience only arises because of a very hateful mind
i.ev: The academic text says patience arises in dependence on a very hateful mind (the enemy's), with no 'only'; the children's text also leaves unclear whose mind it is.
i.fx: Patience arises in dependence on someone's very hateful mind. Since they are the exact cause of patience, they deserve to be honored just like the holy teachings.

atts.t: Therefore, patience arises by depending on someone's very hateful mind. Since they are the exact cause of patience, they deserve to be honored just like the holy teachings.

Living beings have a part in helping me gain every quality of a Buddha. That is why living beings and the Buddhas are seen as equal. But no one is truly equal to the Buddhas. They have an endless ocean of good qualities.

i.sp: a part in helping me gain every quality of a Buddha
i.ev: The academic text says they share in accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha; 'every' and 'helping me' are not there.
i.fx: Living beings have a share in bringing about the qualities of a Buddha.

atts.t: Living beings have a share in bringing about the qualities of a Buddha. Because of this, living beings and the Buddhas are seen as equal. But no one is truly equal to the Buddhas. They have an endless ocean of good qualities.
If even a tiny part of a supreme good quality appears in someone, I should honor them. Even giving them the three realms as a gift would be too little.

i.sp: a tiny part of a supreme good quality
i.ev: The academic text speaks of a fraction of the unique collection of supreme good qualities, and says the offerings are made to that person.
i.fx: If even a tiny part of that special collection of supreme good qualities appears in someone, it would be right to make offerings to them. Even giving them the three realms would be too little.

atts.t: If even a tiny part of that special collection of supreme good qualities appears in someone, I should make offerings to them. Even giving them the three realms would be too little.

i.sp: I should make offerings to them
i.ev: Academic: 'in order to make offerings to them, even offering the three realms would be too little' — a statement of how great the worth is, not an instruction.
i.fx: If even a tiny part of that special collection of supreme good qualities appears in someone, then even offering them the three realms would be too little.

atts.t: The Buddhas are true friends who never trick me. They help me in ways I cannot measure. How could I ever pay them back? The only way is by making living beings happy.

i.sp: The Buddhas are true friends who never trick me.
i.ev: The academic text does not name the Buddhas; it speaks of those who become friends without deceit and perform immeasurable benefit.
i.fx: Those who are true friends who never trick me, and who help me in ways I cannot measure, how could I ever pay them back? The only way is by making living beings happy.

atts.t: There are true friends who never trick me and who help me in ways I cannot measure. How could I ever pay them back? The only way is by making living beings happy.
I will think, "I haven't finished this. I just started that. This is only half done." Then the Lord of Death will suddenly arrive. I will think, "Oh no, I am ruined!"

i.sp: I will think, "I haven't finished this. I just started that. This is only half done." Then the Lord of Death will suddenly arrive.
i.ev: The unfinished state is what he is still in when the Lord of Death suddenly arrives; only then does he think "Alas, I am destroyed!" The children's text puts a first thought before death arrives and then a second thought after.
i.fx: When the Lord of Death suddenly arrives, I will find that "This is not done. That is just begun. This is only half done." Then I will think, "Oh no, I am ruined!"

atts.t: When the Lord of Death suddenly arrives, I will find that "This is not done. That is just begun. This is only half done." Then I will think, "Oh no, I am ruined!"
In this life, you flip around in fear like a live fish out of water. Since you have done harmful deeds, there is no need to mention the unbearable sufferings of hell!

i.sp: like a live fish out of water
i.ev: Only "like a live fish writhing about"; "out of water" is not stated.
i.fx: you flip around in fear like a live fish

atts.t: In this life, you flip around in fear like a live fish. Since you have done harmful deeds, there is no need to even mention the unbearable sufferings of hell!

i.sp: Since you have done harmful deeds, there is no need to even mention the unbearable sufferings of hell!
i.ev: Academic: 'If you ... are possessed by fear in this life, having committed misdeeds, what need is there to mention the unbearable sufferings of hell?' — conditional a fortiori argument (if fear now, how much worse hell); the children's 'Since ... no need to mention' turns it into a flat statement and the idiom can read as hell being unimportant.
i.fx: If you flip around in fear like a live fish even in this life, how much worse will the unbearable sufferings of hell be for someone who has done harmful deeds!

atts.t: Think of flies, mosquitoes, bees, and worms. Even they can build up the power of joyful effort. If they do, they will reach the highest awakening, which is very hard to achieve.

i.sp: mosquitoes
i.ev: The Tibetan/academic text names gadflies, not mosquitoes.
i.fx: Think of flies, gadflies, bees, and worms.

atts.t: Think of flies, gadflies, bees, and worms. If even they build up the power of joyful effort, they will reach the highest awakening, which is very hard to achieve.
I might think, "I am afraid to give away my arms and legs." But this fear is just confusion. I am not thinking about what is truly hard and what is easy.

i.sp: what is truly hard and what is easy
i.ev: The text says "what is heavy and what is light", i.e. weighing the greater against the lesser matter, not what is hard versus easy.
i.fx: I am not weighing what matters more and what matters less.

atts.t: I might think, "I am afraid to give away my arms and legs." But this fear is just confusion. I am not weighing what matters more and what matters less.
The power of the awakening mind wipes out every past harmful deed. It also gathers an ocean of stored goodness. Because of this, the bodhisattva is greater than the Hearers.

i.sp: wipes out every past harmful deed
i.ev: The text says it exhausts previous misdeeds; it does not say "every".
i.fx: The power of the awakening mind uses up past harmful deeds.

atts.t: The power of the awakening mind uses up past harmful deeds. It also gathers an ocean of stored goodness. Because of this, the bodhisattva is greater than the Hearers.
I must build up many good qualities in myself and others. I must practice each and every good quality for an ocean of great ages.

i.sp: I must practice each and every good quality for an ocean of great ages.
i.ev: The sentence is a conditional ("if for each good quality I must familiarize myself for an ocean of eons..."), not a flat statement.
i.fx: If I must practice each and every good quality for an ocean of great ages,

atts.t: I must build up many good qualities in myself and others. If I must practice each and every good quality for an ocean of great ages,
Because I did not have a strong wish for the teachings in the past, and still do not have it now, I have ended up so poor. Who would ever give up a strong wish for the teachings?

i.sp: I have ended up so poor
i.ev: "Destitution" here means lack or misfortune; "poor" may be read as lacking money.
i.fx: I have ended up in such a sad, empty state.

atts.t: Because I did not have a strong wish for the teachings in the past, and still do not have it now, I have ended up in such a sad, empty state. Who would ever give up a strong wish for the teachings?

If I get used to turning back, it will happen in another life too. My harmful deeds and suffering will increase. Any new action and its results will become weak. Then that action will not get finished either.

i.sp: Any new action and its results will become weak.
i.ev: The Tibetan says the 'time of the result' (the ripening time) of the other deed also becomes inferior; the children's text drops 'time of'.
i.fx: Any other action I do, and the time its results come, will become weak.

atts.t: If I get used to giving up, it will happen in another life too. My harmful deeds and suffering will increase. Any other action, and the time of its result, will become weak. Then that other action will not get finished either.

i.sp: If I get used to giving up
i.ev: Academic: 'Habituated to that in another life' - 'that' is not named as giving up in this segment; the children's text supplies a specific referent and shifts the statement into a conditional.
i.fx: If I get used to that in another life too, my harmful deeds and suffering will grow.

atts.t: I should build my pride in three things: my action, my troubling emotions, and my ability. Thinking, "I will do this alone," is called pride in action.

i.sp: I should build my pride in three things: my action, my troubling emotions, and my ability.
i.ev: Text says to cultivate pride in karma, afflictions and capacity (confidence that one can handle them); 'pride in my troubling emotions' can be misread as being proud of them.
i.fx: I should have confidence and pride in three things: my action, my power over troubling emotions, and my ability.

atts.t: I should build my pride in three things: my action, my power over troubling emotions, and my ability. Thinking, "I will do this alone," is pride in action.

i.sp: my power over troubling emotions
i.ev: Academic: 'Karma, afflictions, and capacity: one should cultivate pride in these three.' The segment names afflictions, not power over them.
i.fx: I should build my pride in three things: action, troubling emotions, and my ability.

atts.t: We never get enough of a desire for pleasure, which is like licking honey from a razor's edge. So how could I ever get enough of a store of goodness? Its ripening is happiness and peace.

i.sp: We never get enough of a desire for pleasure, which is like licking honey from a razor's edge.
i.ev: Sensual desires are like honey smeared on a razor's edge; the contrast that merit's ripening is happiness and peace is only implied. Awkward 'a desire for pleasure'.
i.fx: We never get enough of pleasures, which are like honey on a razor's edge. So how could I ever get enough of goodness whose ripening is happiness and peace?

atts.t: If we never get enough of our desires for pleasure, which are like honey smeared on a razor's edge, how could I ever get enough of a store of goodness? Its ripening is happiness and peace.

i.sp: Its ripening is happiness and peace.
i.ev: Academic: merit 'whose ripening is happiness and which is peaceful' - peace describes the store of goodness itself, not its ripening; the rhetorical point (never satiated by goodness) is also blurred by 'how could I ever get enough'.
i.fx: If we never get enough of desires for pleasure, which are like honey on a razor's edge, how could we ever get enough of a store of goodness, which ripens into happiness and is peaceful?

atts.t: Just like a brave warrior fighting enemies with swords on a battlefield, I must dodge the weapons of the troubling emotions. Then I must strike hard to destroy those enemy troubling emotions.

i.sp: brave warrior
i.ev: Tibetan/academic: a veteran (experienced) warrior, not merely a brave one.
i.fx: Just like an experienced warrior fighting enemies with swords on a battlefield

atts.t: Just like an experienced warrior clashing swords with enemies on a battlefield, I must dodge the weapons of the troubling emotions. Then I must strike to destroy those enemy troubling emotions.
From Entering the Way of the Awakening Hero, this is the seventh chapter, called Joyful Effort.

i.sp: called Joyful Effort
i.ev: Title is 'Exposition of Diligence' (brtson 'grus bstan pa); 'Exposition' is dropped.
i.fx: called Teaching on Joyful Effort

atts.t: From Entering the Way of the Awakening Hero, this is the seventh chapter, called the Teaching on Joyful Effort.

terms: Entering the Way of the Awakening Hero

atts.t: If we do not see them, we feel no joy, and the mind does not rest as a settled mind. Even when we do see them, we are never satisfied. We are still hurt by wanting, just as before.

i.sp: the mind does not rest as a settled mind
i.ev: Mind does not rest in meditative equipoise; the phrase is circular and clumsy.
i.fx: the mind cannot become settled

atts.t: If we do not see them, we feel no joy, and the mind cannot become a settled mind. Even when we do see them, we are never satisfied. We are still hurt by wanting, just as before.
If I share the same path as a childish person, I will certainly go to an unhappy realm. If they lead me away from the noble path, what is the use of relying on a childish person?

i.sp: share the same path
i.ev: Text says 'share the same fortune/lot' (skal ba), not path; 'noble path' also reframes 'unlike that of the noble ones'.
i.fx: If I share the same fate as a childish person, I will certainly go to an unhappy realm.

atts.t: If I share the same fate as a childish person, I will certainly go to an unhappy realm. If they lead me to a fate unlike that of the noble ones, what is the use of relying on a childish person?

If I spend time with a childish person, I will hear them praising oneself and putting others down. They will talk happily about the cycle of rebirth. Every kind of bad deed will surely come from this.

i.sp: I will hear them praising oneself
i.ev: Self-praise, the disparagement of others (locked: praising oneself)
i.fx: I will hear them praising themselves and putting others down.

atts.t: If I spend time with a childish person, bad deeds will definitely happen. That childish person brings about praising oneself and putting others down. We will talk about enjoying the cycle of rebirth and things like that.

i.sp: bad deeds will definitely happen. That childish person brings about praising oneself and putting others down.
i.ev: Academic: self-praise, disparaging others and talk delighting in samsara are the examples of non-virtue that will certainly arise in every way; children's text makes them separate things and drops 'in every way'.
i.fx: If I spend time with a childish person, bad deeds will surely come in every way: praising myself, putting others down, and talking about enjoying the cycle of rebirth.

atts.t: If we rely on each other like this, we will only ruin ourselves. They will not do me any good. And I will not do them any good either.

i.sp: we will only ruin ourselves. They will not do me any good. And I will not do them any good either.
i.ev: The ruin follows from the reason: since they do not accomplish my welfare and I will not accomplish theirs.
i.fx: Because they will not do me any good, and I will not do them any good either, we will only ruin ourselves.

atts.t: Because they will not do me any good, and I will not do them any good either, we will only ruin ourselves.

i.ev: Academic: 'when oneself and another rely on each other, by that one will merely come to ruin' - the point that relying on each other leads to ruin is dropped; only the reason clause remains.
i.fx: If we depend on each other like this, we will only come to ruin, because they will not do me any good and I will not do them any good either.

atts.t: A bee just takes nectar from a flower and flies away. In the same way, I will only take what helps me practice the teachings. I will stay slightly apart from everyone, as if I had never met them before.

i.sp: I will stay slightly apart from everyone
i.ev: "I shall remain without familiarity toward everyone" (not becoming close or familiar).
i.fx: I will not become close to anyone, as if I had never met them before.

i.sp: and flies away
i.ev: Bee simply takes nectar from the flower; flying away is not stated.
i.fx: A bee just takes nectar from a flower.

atts.t: A bee just takes nectar from a flower. In the same way, I will only take what helps me practice the teachings. I will not become close to anyone, as if I had never seen them before.

Living beings have many different strong wishes. If even the Victorious Ones cannot please them all, how could an ordinary person like me do it? Therefore, I will let go of my thoughts about the world.

i.sp: an ordinary person like me
i.ev: "an inferior one like me" (self-deprecating, lowly), not merely ordinary.
i.fx: someone as lowly as me

atts.t: Living beings have many different strong wishes. If even the Victorious Ones cannot please them all, how could someone as lowly as me do it? Therefore, I will let go of my thoughts about the world.
In the past, you sent many messengers to win their love. You did not hesitate to do harmful deeds or ruin your good name for them.

i.sp: to win their love
i.ev: Messengers were sent and many requests made for the sake of those people; "winning their love" is not stated.
i.fx: In the past, you sent many messengers and made many requests for their sake.

atts.t: In the past, you sent many messengers and made many requests for their sake. You did not hesitate to do harmful deeds or ruin your good name for them.
When you first lifted the cloth with effort, that face looked down shyly. Whether you had seen it before or not, that face was covered.

i.sp: When you first lifted the cloth with effort, that face looked down shyly.
i.ev: What you first lifted with effort was the face (it looked down out of modesty even when drawn up); the cloth covered it afterward ("that face was covered by a cloth").
i.fx: At first you worked hard to lift that face. Even when you drew it up, it looked down shyly. Whether you had seen it before or not, it was covered by a cloth.

atts.t: At first you worked hard to lift that face. Even when you lifted it up, it looked down shyly. Whether you had seen it before or not, that face was covered by a cloth.
You are full of filth yourself. You carry it around all the time. Yet you still want other bags of filth. You desire them out of greed for filth.

i.sp: You carry it around all the time.
i.ev: The text says you constantly make use of (indulge in) your own impurity, not that you carry it.
i.fx: You use it all the time.

atts.t: You are full of filth yourself. You use it all the time. Yet you still want other bags of filth. You desire them out of greed for filth.
You do not even hate your own filth. But out of greed for filth, you also desire another bag of filth.

i.sp: You do not even hate your own filth.
i.ev: 'Disparage' means look down on or find fault with; 'hate' is stronger.
i.fx: You do not even look down on your own filth.

atts.t: You do not even look down on your own filth. But out of greed for filth, you also desire another bag of filth.
A tiny fraction of that hardship could bring us to the state of a Buddha. A person full of desire goes through suffering worse than the way of acting for awakening. Yet they get no awakening at all.

i.sp: A tiny fraction of that hardship
i.ev: Says a ten-millionth fraction of that hardship; the number is lost.
i.fx: Even a ten-millionth part of that hardship could bring us to the state of a Buddha.

atts.t: Even a ten-millionth part of that hardship could bring us to the state of a Buddha. A person full of desire goes through greater suffering than the way of acting for awakening. Yet they get no awakening at all.
If I act on my own without clinging, I am not tied to anyone at all. The joy of being happy with enough is hard even for Indra to find.

i.sp: If I act on my own without clinging, I am not tied to anyone at all.
i.ev: A general description of one who acts independently and unattached, not a first-person 'if' statement; the verse before uses 'they'.
i.fx: They act on their own without clinging and are not tied to anyone at all.

atts.t: They act on their own without clinging and are not tied to anyone at all. The joy of being happy with enough is hard even for Indra to find.
I should take away the suffering of others. It is suffering, just like my own suffering. I should help other living beings. They are like my very own body.

i.sp: They are like my very own body.
i.ev: The reason is lost: others are to be helped because they are sentient beings, just as my body is (a being I naturally help). The children's text just asserts others are like my body, and drops the 'because'.
i.fx: I should help other living beings, because they are living beings, just like my own body.

atts.t: I should take away the suffering of others, because it is suffering, just like my own suffering. I should help others because they are living beings, just like my own body.
A continuing stream and a collection of parts are not real things. They are just words, like a necklace or an army. Since no one truly owns suffering, who is there to control it?

i.sp: They are just words
i.ev: Academic says the continuum and collection are 'false' (like a garland or army), not 'just words'; this adds a nominalist idea.
i.fx: A continuing stream and a collection of parts are not real in themselves. They are like a necklace or an army.

atts.t: A continuing stream and a collection of parts are not real in themselves. They are like a necklace or an army. Since no one truly owns suffering, who is there to control it?
Someone might ask, "Why should we stop the suffering of everyone?" There is no room to argue. If we stop it, we must stop all of it. If not, then I must suffer just like any other living being.

i.sp: If not, then I must suffer just like any other living being.
i.ev: 'If not, I too am like sentient beings': if suffering need not be averted for all, then mine need not be averted either, since I am one of them. The children's text turns it into an obligation to suffer.
i.fx: If we stop it for anyone, we must stop it for all. If not, then my own suffering should not be stopped either, since I am a living being like them.

atts.t: Someone might ask, "Why should we stop the suffering of everyone?" There is no room to argue. If we stop it, we must stop it for all. If not, then my own suffering should not be stopped either, since I am a living being just like them.
If facing one single suffering removes many other sufferings, a kind person should gladly accept it. They should be willing to bring about that suffering for themselves and others.

i.sp: should gladly accept it
i.ev: 'Gladly' is not in the source; the verse says the compassionate one should certainly take on that suffering.
i.fx: a kind person should certainly take on that suffering for themselves and others.

atts.t: If facing one single suffering removes many other sufferings, a kind person should certainly take on that suffering for themselves and others.
When living beings are freed, there is an ocean of joy. Is that joy not enough? What is the use of wanting freedom just for myself?

i.sp: just for myself
i.ev: The verse asks 'What is the use of desiring liberation?'; 'just for myself' is added interpretation.
i.fx: What is the use of wanting freedom?

atts.t: When living beings are freed, there is an ocean of joy. Is that joy not enough? What is the use of wanting freedom?
I grew used to thinking of drops from others as my own body. Even though they are without a thing that is really me, I call them 'I'.

i.sp: drops from others
i.ev: Source specifies others' drops of semen and blood (the substance of the body) which one habitually takes as 'I'; 'drops from others' loses what the drops are, and 'my own body' / 'really me' are added.
i.fx: By getting used to it, I take the drops of blood and seed that came from others as 'I'. Even though there is no real thing there, I call them 'I'.

atts.t: By getting used to it, I take the drops of seed and blood from others as "I". Even though they are without a thing, I still call them "I".

i.sp: I take the drops of seed and blood from others as "I". Even though they are without a thing, I still call them "I".
i.ev: The Tibetan has a comparison ("just as one knows them as 'I'"): by habit, others' drops of semen and blood, though no real entity, are known as "I". The children's text turns the simile into two flat statements.
i.fx: By getting used to it, even the drops of seed and blood that came from others, which are without a thing, are known as "I".

atts.t: If I only wish to be great, I will be reborn in an unhappy realm as someone low and foolish. If I shift that wish to others, I will gain a happy realm and respect.

i.sp: only
i.ev: Source says wishing for oneself to be exalted; 'only' is not there.
i.fx: If I wish to be great myself, I will be reborn in an unhappy realm as someone low and foolish.

atts.t: If I wish to be great myself, I will be reborn in an unhappy realm as someone low and foolish. If I shift that wish to others, I will gain a happy realm and respect.
If I do not exchange my own happiness for the suffering of others, I will never reach the state of a Buddha. Even in the cycle of rebirth, I will find no happiness.

i.ev: 'Truly' exchange (yang dag par) is dropped.
i.fx: If I do not truly exchange my own happiness for the suffering of others, ...

atts.t: If I do not truly exchange my own happiness for the suffering of others, I will never reach the state of a Buddha. Even in the cycle of rebirth, I will find no happiness.
Out of confusion, I might cause suffering to others. This only brings me unbearable suffering. I throw away the perfect joy that brings happiness I can see and cannot see.

i.sp: I might cause suffering to others
i.ev: Academic: one abandons joy through the cause of inflicting suffering on others; the harm is a stated fact, not a possibility ('might').
i.fx: Out of confusion, I cause suffering to others. This only brings me unbearable suffering, and I throw away the perfect joy that brings happiness I can see and cannot see.

atts.t: Out of confusion, I cause suffering to others. This brings me unbearable suffering, and I throw away the perfect joy that brings happiness I can see and cannot see.

i.sp: happiness I can see and cannot see
i.ev: Academic: "seen and unseen happiness" (happiness in this life and beyond); the phrasing is hard for children to parse.
i.fx: ...the perfect joy that brings happiness now and happiness we cannot yet see.

atts.t: Pretend that you are someone lower. Pretend that others are you. Clear your mind of busy thinking. Then practice feeling jealousy, rivalry, and pride.

i.sp: Pretend that you are someone lower. Pretend that others are you.
i.ev: Academic: 'Having made the inferior and so forth into oneself, and having made oneself into others'. The inferior (and equal, etc.) are made into oneself, and oneself into the others; the children's text reverses the direction of both exchanges and drops 'and so forth'.
i.fx: See the lower person as yourself, and see yourself as the other person. Clear your mind of busy thinking. Then practice feeling jealousy, rivalry, and pride.

atts.t: See a lower person and others as yourself. Then see yourself as them. Clear your mind of busy thinking. Practice feeling jealousy, rivalry, and pride.

i.sp: See a lower person and others as yourself.
i.ev: Academic: "the inferior and so forth" (inferior, equal, superior). "And others" is vague and could be read as ordinary other people.
i.fx: See someone lower, equal, or higher than you as yourself.

atts.t: In short, think of any harm you have ever done to others for your own sake. Now, for the sake of all living beings, let that harm fall upon yourself.

i.sp: think of any harm you have ever done
i.ev: Academic: 'Whatever harm you have done to others... let that harm descend upon yourself' — a command to let the harm fall on oneself, not to recall it.
i.fx: In short, whatever harm you have done to others for your own sake, let that same harm fall upon yourself, for the sake of all living beings.

atts.t: In short, whatever harm you have done to others for your own sake, let that same harm fall upon yourself, for the sake of all living beings.
Even when I tell you what to do, if you do not listen, my mind, I must defeat you. All faults come from you, so I have no other choice.

i.sp: All faults come from you
i.ev: Academic: 'all faults rely upon you' (faults depend on / dwell in the mind), not that they originate from it; also 'do not act like that' is softened to 'do not listen'.
i.fx: Even when I tell you what to do, if you, my mind, do not act that way, I must defeat you. All faults rely on you, so I have no other choice.

atts.t: Even when I tell you what to do, if you, my mind, do not act that way, I must defeat you. All faults rely on you, so I have no other choice.

i.sp: I must defeat you
i.ev: Academic: "subdue you yourself" (Tibetan ཚར་གཅད, to bring under control/discipline). "Defeat" suggests winning a fight.
i.fx: I must bring you under control.

atts.t: That past time when you ruined me is over. Now I see you. Where will you go? I will destroy all your feeling superior.

i.sp: I will destroy all your feeling superior.
i.ev: Ungrammatical use of the locked term as a noun phrase; Tibetan/academic: 'I shall destroy all your haughtiness'.
i.fx: I will destroy all of your feeling superior, every bit of it.

atts.t: That past time when you ruined me is over. Now I see you. Where will you go? I will destroy all of your feeling superior.

i.sp: destroy all of your feeling superior
i.ev: Locked term "feeling superior" is used as a noun phrase, making the sentence ungrammatical.
i.fx: I will destroy all of your feeling of being better than others.

atts.t: You have handed me over to suffering again and again. I have hurt for a long time. I remember those grudges. Now I will destroy your thoughts about your own good.

i.sp: handed me over to suffering
i.ev: The academic text says only "handed me over time and again"; no object such as suffering is stated.
i.fx: You have handed me over again and again. I have suffered for a long time.

atts.t: In that way, you have handed me over again and again. I have suffered for a long time. I remember those grudges. Now I will destroy your thoughts about your own good.
So, without being attached, I will give up my body to help others. It has many faults. Still, I will keep it like a tool for doing good.

i.sp: a tool for doing good
i.ev: Academic: "an instrument for action" (ལས་ཀྱི་སྤྱད); "for doing good" is not stated.
i.fx: I will keep it like a tool for getting things done.

atts.t: So, without being attached, I will give up my body to help others. It has many faults. Still, I will keep it like a tool for getting things done.

Even a meditation master has a different level of thinking mind. Higher masters prove the lower ones wrong. They use examples they both agree on. They do not question these examples because they just want a result.

i.sp: Even a meditation master has a different level of thinking mind.
i.ev: Academic: yogis differ from one another in intellect, and are refuted by those successively higher; the children's line reads as if one master differs from something unnamed.
i.fx: Meditation masters are not all equal in their thinking minds. A higher master proves a lower one wrong.

atts.t: Meditation masters are not all equal in their thinking minds. A higher master proves a lower one wrong. They use examples they both agree on. They do not question these examples because they just want a result.

Someone might say, "Since even a Buddha would be trapped in the world, what is the use of the way of acting for awakening?" I reply: As long as the unbroken flow of circumstances is not cut, even an illusion will not stop.

i.sp: trapped in the world
i.ev: Academic: "even a Buddha would cycle [in saṃsāra]"; the locked term for འཁོར་བ is "cycle of rebirth", while "world" is locked for འཇིག་རྟེན.
i.fx: Since even a Buddha would keep going around in the cycle of rebirth, what is the use of the way of acting for awakening?

atts.t: Someone might say, "Since even a Buddha would keep going around in the cycle of rebirth, what is the use of the way of acting for awakening?" I reply: As long as the unbroken flow of circumstances is not cut, even an illusion will not stop.

Someone might say, "Because of a special circumstance, a person can see that the mind shines to itself." But using magic eye ointment lets you see a hidden vase. It does not let you see the eye ointment itself.

i.sp: Because of a special circumstance, a person can see that the mind shines to itself.
i.ev: Academic: the opponent argues that because the mind, endowed with other conditions, sees (objects), it is luminous to itself. The children's text says a person sees the mind shining, and turns "other conditions" into a "special circumstance".
i.fx: Someone might say, "The mind has other circumstances to help it see, so it shines to itself."

i.sp: a hidden vase
i.ev: Academic: "the vase is seen"; nothing says the vase was hidden.
i.fx: lets you see a vase

atts.t: Someone might say, "Because the mind uses other circumstances to see, it shines to itself." Using magic eye ointment lets you see a vase. But it does not let you see the eye ointment itself.
But if a non-existent thing depends on a real thing, how could it do anything? Without anything outside it, your mind would have no companion. Your mind would become completely alone.

i.sp: Without anything outside it
i.ev: Academic: 'Your mind, without a companion, would become entirely solitary.' Nothing about 'outside it'.
i.fx: Your mind would have no companion. It would be completely alone.

atts.t: If a non-existent thing depends on a thing, how could it do anything? Your mind would have no companion. It would be completely alone.
When you say, "This thing does not exist," and you cannot find the thing you are looking for, what happens? How can a non-existent thing without a base stay in front of the thinking mind?

i.sp: the thing you are looking for
i.ev: Academic: 'the entity to be analyzed is not apprehended' (the thing being examined, not found).
i.fx: and you look closely at the thing and cannot find it

atts.t: When you say, "This does not exist," and you look closely at the thing but cannot find it, what happens? How can a non-existent thing without a base stay in front of the thinking mind?
In the same way, following the way of acting for awakening, the shrine of the Victorious One has been built. Even after the awakening hero passes away, it still achieves every goal.

i.sp: passes away
i.ev: Tibetan/academic: the bodhisattva 'has passed into nirvāṇa' (mya ngan las 'das); the glossary renders this as 'freedom from sorrow' (as in 9-38).
i.fx: Even after the awakening hero passes into freedom from sorrow, it still achieves every goal.

atts.t: In the same way, following the way of acting for awakening, the shrine of the Victorious One has been built. Even after the awakening hero passes into freedom from sorrow, it still achieves every goal.
Someone might ask, "If the Great Vehicle is not proven, how is your sacred text proven?" You might answer, "Because we both agree on it." But at first, it was not proven for you either.

i.sp: You might answer, "Because we both agree on it." But at first, it was not proven for you either.
i.ev: Academic puts 'Because this is established for both of us' in a separate quotation from the opponent's question (a different speaker), then 'Initially this was not established for you'; children's text has the opponent answer and adds 'either'.
i.fx: Someone might ask, "If the Great Vehicle is not proven, how is your sacred text proven?" The answer is, "Because it is proven for both of us." But at first, it was not proven for you.

atts.t: Someone might ask, "If the Great Vehicle is not proven, how is your sacred text proven?" The answer is, "Because it is proven for both of us." But at first, it was not proven for you.

Someone might say, "We reject the Great Vehicle because people argue about it." But you argue with a non-Buddhist about your sacred text. You also argue with other groups about other sacred texts. Since people argue about them, you would have to throw them all away.

i.sp: You also argue with other groups about other sacred texts.
i.ev: Academic: for other scriptures there is dispute 'with your own and other schools'; 'your own' groups is dropped.
i.fx: You also argue about other sacred texts, both with your own groups and with other groups.

atts.t: Someone might say, "We reject the Great Vehicle because people argue about it." But you argue with a non-Buddhist about your sacred text. You also argue about other sacred texts, both with your own groups and with other groups. Since people argue about them, you would have to throw them all away.
If being a monk is the root of the teaching, even being a monk is hard to prove. For people whose minds are holding on to things, even freedom from sorrow is hard to reach.

i.sp: hard to reach
i.ev: Academic: nirvāṇa is 'difficult to establish', same wording as the monk clause ('hard to prove'); 'reach' shifts the point from establishing to attaining.
i.fx: even freedom from sorrow is hard to prove

atts.t: If being a monk is the root of the teaching, even being a monk is hard to prove. For people whose minds are holding on to things, even freedom from sorrow is hard to prove.

Someone might say it is certain that, for now, the wanting that causes holding on does not exist. Even if that wanting is not troubled by troubling emotion, why would it not exist? It would be just like confusion.

i.sp: It would be just like confusion.
i.ev: Academic: 'Why would it not exist, just like delusion?' - a comparison inside the question (craving exists just as delusion does), not a flat statement.
i.fx: Why would it not exist, just as confusion still exists?

atts.t: Someone might say it is certain that, for now, the wanting that causes holding on does not exist. Even if that wanting is not troubled by troubling emotion, why would it not exist, just as confusion still exists?
A mind that does not have emptiness will start up again even after it stops. It is like a deep meditation with no perceiving. Because of this, you should meditate on emptiness.

i.sp: does not have emptiness
i.ev: Academic: 'devoid of emptiness' means a mind without the realization of emptiness; 'does not have emptiness' suggests emptiness is something to possess.
i.fx: A mind that has not understood emptiness will start up again even after it stops.

atts.t: A mind that has not understood emptiness will start up again even after it stops. It is like a deep meditation with no perceiving. Because of this, you should meditate on emptiness.
You say that leaving out one text makes them all faulty. But what if one is like a true teaching text? Why are they not all spoken by the Victorious One?

i.sp: a true teaching text
i.ev: Academic: 'a single one similar to a sūtra' - no 'true'.
i.fx: what if just one is like a teaching text

atts.t: You say that leaving out one text makes them all faulty. But if just one is like a teaching text, why are they not all spoken by the Victorious One?

i.sp: leaving out one text
i.ev: Academic: "a single unincluded one" (one text not included among the accepted teachings); "leaving out" is vague and the final "all" is unclear.
i.fx: You say that if one text is not counted as the Buddha's teaching, then all of them are faulty.

atts.t: We want to help those who have suffering from confusion. So, we are freed from extreme clinging and fear. We can now stay in the cycle of rebirth. This is the result of emptiness.

i.sp: We want to help those who have suffering from confusion. So, we are freed from extreme clinging and fear.
i.ev: Academic: for the sake of those suffering through delusion, one freed from the extremes of attachment and fear remains in saṃsāra. No 'we want', and being freed is not caused by wanting to help ('So' invents the logic); 'extreme clinging' misses 'the extremes of attachment and fear'.
i.fx: For the sake of those who suffer from confusion, a person who is free from the extremes of clinging and fear can stay in the cycle of rebirth. This is the result of emptiness.

atts.t: For the sake of those who experience suffering from confusion, a person who is free from the extremes of clinging and fear can stay in the cycle of rebirth. This is the result of emptiness.
Teeth, hair, and nails are not the self, and the self is not bones or blood. It is not mucus or phlegm, and it is not lymph or pus.

i.sp: lymph
i.ev: Hard unexplained word for ages 8-12 (Tibetan chu ser, a body fluid).
i.fx: a watery body fluid

atts.t: Teeth, hair, and nails are not the self, and the self is not bones or blood. It is not mucus or phlegm, and it is not a watery body fluid or pus.
If something is made to notice a sound, how could it become the thing that notices a shape? One person can be labelled as both a father and a son. But that is not what is truly real.

i.sp: If something is made to notice a sound
i.ev: Academic: 'Whatever has the nature of apprehending sound' - a nature, not something 'made to' do it.
i.fx: If something has the nature of noticing a sound, how could it also be the thing that notices a shape?

atts.t: If something has the nature of noticing a sound, how could it become the thing that notices a shape? One person can be labelled as both a father and a son. But that is not what is truly real.

Someone might say it is like an actor playing a new part. But if that thing changes, it is not lasting forever. If that new part is the exact same thing, then this kind of oneness is completely unheard of.

i.sp: Someone might say it is like an actor playing a new part.
i.ev: The verse is Santideva's own reply: if the thing is seen in another mode like an actor, it is not permanent; nobody is quoted as an opponent here.
i.fx: If it is like an actor who shows up in a new way, then we see it changing, so it is not lasting forever.

atts.t: If it is like an actor who shows up in a new way, then we see it changing, so it is not lasting forever. If that new way is the exact same thing, then this kind of oneness has never been seen before.
A thing without a mind is not the self. It is just like a vase. But you might say it knows things because it gets a mind. Then the thing that did not know anything before would be destroyed.

i.sp: A thing without a mind is not the self. It is just like a vase.
i.ev: The reason is given: it is not the self because it is mindless, like a vase and so on.
i.fx: A thing without a mind is not the self, because it has no mind, just like a vase.

atts.t: A thing without a mind is not the self, because it has no mind, just like a vase. But you might say it knows things because it gets a mind. Then the thing that did not know anything before would be destroyed.
Someone might ask, "If there are no living beings, who should we show compassion to?" We show compassion to those imagined by our confusion. We accept this confusion for the sake of the result.

i.sp: We accept this confusion for the sake of the result.
i.ev: What is accepted for the sake of the result is the thing imputed by delusion (the imagined beings), not the delusion itself.
i.fx: We show compassion to beings imagined by our confusion. We accept them like this for the sake of the result.

atts.t: Someone might ask, "If there are no living beings, who should we show compassion to?" We show compassion to those imagined by our confusion. We accept them for the sake of the result.
It is not the body, and it is not anywhere else. It is not mixed with anything, and it is not separate. It is nothing at all. Because of this, every living being is in freedom from sorrow by nature.

i.sp: It is not the body, and it is not anywhere else. ... It is nothing at all.
i.ev: The subject is the mind of the previous verse; with no named subject, 'It is nothing at all' can read as a claim that nothing exists.
i.fx: The mind is not the body, and it is not anywhere else. It is not mixed with anything, and it is not separate. It cannot be found as anything at all.

atts.t: The mind is not the body, and it is not anywhere else. It is not mixed with anything, and it is not separate. It cannot be found as anything at all. Because of this, every living being is in freedom from sorrow by nature.

i.sp: The mind is not the body
i.ev: Source says only "That which is not the body, nor anywhere else..."; it does not name the mind as the subject.
i.fx: Whatever is not the body and is not anywhere else, is not mixed with anything, and is not separate, cannot be found as anything at all. Because of this, every living being is in freedom from sorrow by nature.

atts.t: Imagining and the thing imagined depend on each other. We can only share our careful examinations by relying on what people already know.

i.sp: We can only share our careful examinations
i.ev: "All analyses are expressed" relying on what is commonly known; no "only" and no idea of sharing.
i.fx: Every careful examination is spoken by relying on what people already know.

atts.t: Imagining and the thing imagined depend on each other. Every careful examination is spoken by relying on what people already know.
People who believe in a never-changing atom have already been proven wrong. The Samkhya thinkers say that a never-changing Primal Matter is the cause of beings.

i.sp: a never-changing atom
i.ev: "permanent atoms" (plural: those who assert never-changing atoms).
i.fx: People who believe in never-changing atoms have already been proven wrong.

atts.t: People who believe in never-changing atoms have already been proven wrong. The Samkhya thinkers say that a never-changing Primal Matter is the cause of beings.
You might say happiness and other feelings come from things like cloth. Since those things do not exist, happiness does not exist either. Also, we never see happiness as something never-changing.

i.sp: You might say
i.ev: The verse states "Happiness and so forth arise from cloth and so forth" without framing it as an opponent's claim; the next line then draws the conclusion.
i.fx: Happiness and other feelings would come from things like cloth. Since those things do not exist, happiness does not exist either.

atts.t: Happiness and other feelings would come from things like cloth. Since those things do not exist, happiness does not exist either. Also, we never see happiness as something never-changing.
Sometimes a thing is seen only because something else is near. When that other thing is gone, it is not seen. It is made up, just like a reflection. How could being truly real happen in that?

i.sp: Sometimes a thing is seen
i.ev: "Whatever is seen through the proximity of something" - applies to anything, not just some cases.
i.fx: Whatever is seen only because something else is near, and is not seen when that is gone, is made up, like a reflection.

atts.t: Whatever is seen only because something else is near, and is unseen when that is gone, is made up. It is like a reflection. How could being truly real exist in that?
Even millions of causes cannot change a non-existent thing. How could a non-existent thing ever become real? And what else could become a thing?

i.sp: Even millions of causes
i.ev: Tibetan/academic: hundreds of millions of causes (བྱེ་བ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག); the number is scaled down.
i.fx: Even hundreds of millions of causes cannot change a non-existent thing.

atts.t: Even hundreds of millions of causes cannot change a non-existent thing. How could that state be a thing? And what else could become a thing?
So, there is no stopping, and there is no thing. Therefore, all these beings are always never born and never ending.

i.sp: all these beings are always never born and never ending
i.ev: Double adverb/negation is tangled for ages 8-12; academic: always unborn and unceasing.
i.fx: Therefore all these beings are always never born and never ending.

atts.t: So, there is no stopping, and there is no thing. Therefore, all these beings are always never born and never ending.

i.sp: are always never born and never ending
i.ev: Source: always unborn and unceasing; locked term is 'never born and never ending'.
i.fx: all these beings are never born and never ending, always.

atts.t: I hope people like me completely understand that everything is like space. People who want happiness for themselves find causes for fighting and excitement.

i.sp: find causes for fighting and excitement
i.ev: Academic: those who desire happiness for themselves, through causes of conflict and excitement, (next verse) become greatly agitated and delighted; the causes act on them, they do not 'find' them.
i.fx: People who want happiness only for themselves are stirred up by fighting and excitement

atts.t: May people like me completely understand that everything is like space. People who want happiness for themselves are stirred up by causes of fighting and excitement.

In life, there are many steep cliffs. There, what is not the way things really are is like this. Because things clash with each other there, in life there is no such thing as the way things really are.

i.sp: There, what is not the way things really are is like this. Because things clash with each other there, in life there is no such thing as the way things really are.
i.ev: Tangled, abstract sentences; academic: what is not reality is like this; because of mutual contradiction there, there is no such reality in existence.
i.fx: Life has many steep cliffs, and what is false looks like this. Because things clash with each other, there is no true way things really are in life.

atts.t: Life has many steep cliffs, and what is false looks like this. Because things clash with each other, there is no such thing as the way things really are in life.
In that place, the ocean of suffering is huge and too hard to bear. It has no edge. There, people have very little strength, and their lives are short.

i.ev: Academic: 'incomparable' (དཔེ་མེད) ocean of suffering is lost; 'huge' replaces it.
i.fx: In that place, the ocean of suffering has nothing to compare with it, is too hard to bear, and has no edge.

atts.t: In that place, the ocean of suffering has nothing to compare with it. It is too hard to bear and has no edge. There, people have very little strength, and their lives are short.

Through my roots of good deeds, may the living beings of hell see Samantabhadra and other awakening heroes. These heroes bring happy clouds and let a cool, sweet-smelling rain fall. When the living beings see this, may they be filled with joy.

i.ev: Academic: the bodhisattvas' clouds are 'unobstructed' (སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད); this is dropped.
i.fx: These heroes bring happy clouds that nothing blocks, and let a cool, sweet-smelling rain fall.

atts.t: Through my roots of good deeds, may the living beings of hell see Samantabhadra and other awakening heroes. These heroes bring happy clouds that nothing blocks, and let a cool, sweet-smelling rain fall. When the living beings see this, may they be filled with joy.
May poor people find wealth. May very sad people find joy. May those who feel hopeless get their spirit back and become perfectly strong.

i.sp: become perfectly strong
i.ev: 'attain perfect steadfastness' (stable, firm in mind), not physical strength
i.fx: and become perfectly steady and firm

atts.t: May poor people find wealth. May very sad people find joy. May those who feel hopeless get their spirit back and become perfectly steady and firm.
May any living beings who lack brightness shine with great brightness. May any persons of hard practice who look weak get beautiful and perfect bodies.

i.sp: who look weak
i.ev: 'poor forms' means unattractive appearance, not weakness
i.fx: who look plain get beautiful and perfect bodies

atts.t: May any living beings who lack brightness shine with great brightness. May any persons of hard practice who look plain get beautiful and perfect bodies.
May all the women in the world become men. May lowly people reach high places, but may their pride be defeated.

i.sp: reach high places
i.ev: 'attain high status' (rank), not physical places
i.fx: reach high status

atts.t: May all the women in the world become men. May lowly people reach high status, and may their pride be defeated.
A good thinking mind comes from his kindness. I bow down to Manjushri. I have grown because of his kindness. I also bow down to the good friend.

i.sp: A good thinking mind comes from his kindness. ... I have grown because of his kindness.
i.ev: 'Through whose kindness' refers to Manjushri in the first pair and to the good friend in the second; the children's text uses 'his' before either person is named, so the second 'his' reads as Manjushri rather than the good friend.
i.fx: Thanks to Manjushri's kindness, a good thinking mind comes to me. I bow down to Manjushri. Thanks to the good friend's kindness, I have grown. I also bow down to the good friend.

atts.t: Thanks to Manjushri's kindness, a good thinking mind comes to me. I bow down to Manjushri. Thanks to the good friend's kindness, I have grown. I also bow down to the good friend.
Even later, it was carefully fixed, translated, and perfectly finished by the Indian teacher who ordained me, Sumatikirti, and the chief editor-translator, the monk Loden Sherab.

i.sp: carefully fixed
i.ev: The academic translation says 'correctly revised' (dag par bcos), meaning corrected to be accurate, not done with care.
i.fx: Even later, it was fixed so it was correct, translated, and perfectly finished by ...

atts.t: Even later, it was fixed so it was correct, translated, and perfectly finished by the Indian teacher who ordained me, Sumatikirti, and the chief editor-translator, the monk Loden Sherab.

i.sp: the Indian teacher who ordained me, Sumatikirti
i.ev: Academic: 'the Indian preceptor Sumatikirti'; 'me' is not in the source and wrongly suggests the narrator was ordained by him (locked term was applied literally).
i.fx: the Indian teacher who ordains monks, Sumatikirti

atts.t: 就像在漆黑夜晚的烏雲裡，一瞬間的閃電會照亮一切。同樣地，靠著佛陀的力量，世界上想要得到累積的福氣的智慧，偶爾才會出現一次。

i.sp: 世界上想要得到累積的福氣的智慧
i.ev: Academic: the wisdom of cultivating merit (修福德之慧) arises only occasionally, once in a hundred times; the children's text turns it into wisdom that "wants to obtain" merit and loses "among a hundred (moments)".
i.fx: 靠著佛陀的力量，世界上想要累積福氣的好念頭，在一百次裡偶爾才會出現一次。

atts.t: 就像在漆黑夜晚的烏雲裡，一瞬間的閃電會照亮一切。同樣地，靠著佛陀的力量，世界上想要獲得累積的福氣的智慧，在一百次裡偶爾才會出現一次。

i.sp: 想要獲得累積的福氣的智慧
i.ev: The Tibetan/academic text speaks of the wisdom/intelligence that cultivates merit ("修福德之慧"), not wanting to obtain it; wording is also tangled.
i.fx: 世界上想要去累積福氣的智慧，在一百次裡偶爾才會出現一次。

atts.t: 覺悟之心就像最神奇的變金子的藥水。它能把我們不乾淨的身體，變成得勝者那樣無價的寶石，也就是得勝者的身體。所以，一定要緊緊抓牢這顆覺悟之心。

i.sp: 變成得勝者那樣無價的寶石，也就是得勝者的身體
i.ev: Academic: the impure body is transformed into a priceless jewel, namely the body of the Victor; the children's text makes it sound like a jewel "like the Victor".
i.fx: 它能把我們不乾淨的身體，變成無價的寶石，也就是得勝者的身體。

atts.t: 覺悟之心就像最神奇的變金子的藥水。它能把我們不乾淨的身體，變成無價的寶石，也就是得勝者的身體。所以，一定要緊緊抓牢這顆覺悟之心。
佛陀就像眾生唯一的商隊的領隊。他用無比的智慧仔細觀察，發現這顆心極為珍貴。想要脫離眾生受苦的地方，就要好好守護這顆珍貴的覺悟之心。

i.sp: 佛陀就像眾生唯一的商隊的領隊
i.ev: Academic: "the sole caravan-leader of beings" with immeasurable wisdom; the Buddha is not named and no simile is stated.
i.fx: 眾生唯一的商隊的領隊，用無比的智慧仔細觀察，發現這顆心極為珍貴。

atts.t: 眾生唯一的商隊的領隊，用無比的智慧仔細觀察，發現這顆心極為珍貴。想要脫離眾生受苦的地方，就要好好守護這顆珍貴的覺悟之心。

i.sp: 脫離眾生受苦的地方
i.ev: The text says only "desire to be free from the state/place of beings"; "suffering" is not stated.
i.fx: 想要脫離眾生所在的地方，就要好好守護這顆珍貴的覺悟之心。

atts.t: 就算做了非常可怕的有害的行為。只要依靠它就能立刻得救。就像依靠勇士逃離巨大的危險。小心謹慎的人為什麼不依靠它呢？

i.sp: 就算做了非常可怕的有害的行為。只要依靠它就能立刻得救。
i.ev: Fragmented sentence; "它" (bodhicitta) is not named in this segment, so a child cannot tell what to rely on. Academic: even one who has done unbearable wrongdoing is freed in an instant by relying on that (bodhicitta).
i.fx: 就算做了非常可怕的有害的行為，只要依靠覺悟之心，也能立刻得救，就像依靠勇士逃離巨大的危險。

atts.t: 就算做了非常可怕的有害的行為，只要依靠覺悟之心就能立刻得救，就像依靠勇士逃離巨大的危險。小心謹慎的人，為什麼不依靠它呢？
它就像世界末日的大火。能在一瞬間燒毀巨大的過錯。它有數不清的好處。有智慧的彌勒守護者，已經對善財說過這些了。

i.sp: 它就像世界末日的大火。
i.ev: Referent "它" (bodhicitta) is unnamed in this segment; academic also says the great wrongdoings are "certainly" burned in an instant, which is not stated.
i.fx: 覺悟之心就像世界末日的大火，一瞬間就一定能燒毀巨大的過錯。

atts.t: 覺悟之心就像世界末日的大火，一瞬間就一定能燒毀巨大的過錯。它有數不清的好處，有智慧的彌勒守護者已經對善財說過這些了。
有了想要覺悟的心願。雖然在輪迴時能產生巨大的結果。但它不像動身去覺悟的心那樣。能讓累積的福氣不斷地產生。

i.sp: 有了想要覺悟的心願。雖然在輪迴時能產生巨大的結果。
i.ev: Broken sentences; the concessive "although...but not like" structure is split into fragments. Academic is one connected comparison.
i.fx: 想要覺悟的心願，雖然在輪迴時也能帶來巨大的結果，但不像動身去覺悟的心那樣，能讓累積的福氣不斷地產生。

atts.t: 想要覺悟的心願，雖然在輪迴時能產生巨大的結果，但不像動身去覺悟的心那樣，能讓累積的福氣不斷地產生。
為了拯救無邊無際的眾生領域。我們用不再回頭的心。真正去接受這種心。從那一刻開始。

i.sp: 為了拯救無邊無際的眾生領域。我們用不再回頭的心。真正去接受這種心。從那一刻開始。
i.ev: Fragmented across four sentences, with "眾生領域" a hard phrase; academic is one clause: from the time one truly takes up that mind with an irreversible resolve to liberate the boundless realm of beings.
i.fx: 從我們為了解脫無邊無際的眾生，用不再回頭的心，真正接受這顆覺悟之心的那一刻開始，

atts.t: 從我們為了解脫無邊無際的眾生領域，用不再回頭的心，真正去接受這顆覺悟之心的那一刻開始，
在妙臂請問如來的時候，如來為了幫助信心不足的眾生，親自講述了這個道理。

i.sp: 信心不足的眾生
i.ev: Academic: beings of inferior inclination/aspiration (下劣信解); this is about their limited aspiration, not lack of faith.
i.fx: 心願還不夠寬廣的眾生

i.ev: Academic: "此者連同其正理" - the teaching was given together with its reasoning; the reasoning is not mentioned.
i.fx: 如來為了幫助心願還不夠寬廣的眾生，親自把這個道理和理由一起講了出來。

atts.t: 在妙臂請問如來的時候，如來為了幫助心願還不夠寬廣的眾生，親自把這個道理和理由一起講了出來。
如果有人只給少數眾生一點食物。他只花短短的時間給一頓飯。就算他態度傲慢只讓人吃半飽。世人還是會尊敬他做了好事。

i.sp: 只讓人吃半飽
i.ev: Academic: the giver satisfies (them) for only half a day (令飽半日), a limited duration; "half full" changes a time span into an amount.
i.fx: 就算他帶著輕視，只讓人飽上半天。

i.sp: 只給少數眾生一點食物
i.ev: Academic: he supplies food to a few beings continuously (持續供應飲食); the continuity is lost.
i.fx: 如果有人持續給少數眾生食物。

atts.t: 如果有人只給少數眾生一點食物。他只花短短的時間給一頓飯。就算他帶著輕視，只讓人飽上半天。世人還是會尊敬他做了好事。

i.ev: The giving of food and drink is continuous ("持續供應飲食"); the children's text drops the continuous provision and only says "a little food".
i.fx: 如果有人一直給少數眾生一點飲食，卻只在短短的時間裡給一頓飯，還帶著輕視，只讓人飽上半天，世人還是會尊敬他做了好事。

i.sp: 如果有人只給少數眾生一點食物。他只花短短的時間給一頓飯。就算他帶著輕視
i.ev: The conditional is broken into separate sentences by full stops, leaving "如果...。" and "就算..." ungrammatical.
i.fx: 如果有人給少數眾生一點食物，只花短短的時間給一頓飯，還帶著輕視，只讓人飽上半天，世人還是會尊敬他做了好事。

atts.t: 為了在心中保持那顆珍貴的心，我要準備美好的禮物來供養。我要供養如來和神聖的佛法，他們是純潔無瑕的珍寶。我也要供養佛陀的孩子，他們擁有美好品質的大海。

i.sp: 我要供養如來和神聖的佛法,他們是純潔無瑕的珍寶。我也要供養佛陀的孩子,他們擁有美好品質的大海。
i.ev: Tibetan/academic list four offering objects: the Tathagatas, the sacred Dharma, the stainless Jewel, and the Buddha's children, all of them "oceans of good qualities". The children's text turns "stainless jewel" into a description of the first two and gives "ocean of qualities" only to the Buddha's children.
i.fx: 我要供養如來、神聖的佛法、純潔無瑕的珍寶，還有佛陀的孩子。他們都像美好品質的大海。

atts.t: 為了在心中保持那顆珍貴的心，我要準備美好的禮物來供養。我要供養如來、神聖的佛法、純潔無瑕的珍寶，還有佛陀的孩子。他們都像美好品質的大海。
他們擁有美好品質的大海。我要用無數好聽的聲音讚美他們。希望這些好聽的聲音像雲一樣，不斷飄到他們身邊。

i.sp: 他們擁有美好品質的大海。
i.ev: The verse opens "to the oceans of good qualities, I praise with oceans of praise-sounds"; the children's opening sentence has no antecedent for "他們".
i.fx: 他們是美好品質的大海。我要用像大海一樣多的好聽聲音讚美他們。

atts.t: 他們是美好品質的大海。我要用像大海一樣多的好聽聲音讚美他們。希望這些好聽的聲音像雲一樣，不斷飄到他們身邊。
在有害的行為被洗淨之前，我也許就會先死去了。為了讓我得到確實的自由，請趕快來救護我。

i.sp: 我也許就會先死去了
i.ev: Academic: "before my wrongdoing is purified, I will die first" (stated as certain); the children's "也許" (perhaps) adds uncertainty.
i.fx: 在有害的行為被洗淨之前，我就會先死去了。

atts.t: 在有害的行為被洗淨之前，我就會先死去了。為了讓我得到確實的自由，請趕快來救護我。
就算只是在這一輩子裡，許多親友和討厭的人已經死去了。但是我為了他們而做了有害的行為，這些難以忍受的後果還留在我的面前。

i.sp: 這些難以忍受的後果還留在我的面前
i.ev: The unbearable wrongdoings (sins) done for them remain before me; the text speaks of the harmful acts themselves, not "consequences".
i.fx: 但是我為了他們做的那些難以忍受的有害行為，還留在我的面前。

atts.t: 就在我活著的這一生中，許多親友和敵人都已經過世了。但是，我為了他們而做出的那些可怕的有害的行為，卻全都留在我的面前。
他們領悟了佛法，能消除輪迴的恐懼。對於這些佛法，以及所有的菩薩們，我也同樣真心地尋求庇護。

i.sp: 他們領悟了佛法，能消除輪迴的恐懼。對於這些佛法
i.ev: Academic: the Dharma they realized, which removes the fear of samsara; the subject of 'removes' is the Dharma, but the children's sentence reads as if 'they' remove it, and the repeated 'these Dharma' is clumsy.
i.fx: 佛陀們領悟的佛法，能消除輪迴的恐懼。我也同樣真心地向這些佛法，還有所有的菩薩們，尋求庇護。

atts.t: 佛陀們領悟的佛法，能消除輪迴的恐懼。我也同樣真心地向這些佛法，還有所有的菩薩們，尋求庇護。
我都要來到守護者面前，因為害怕痛苦而雙手合十。我一次又一次鞠躬敬禮，坦承這一切。

i.sp: 我都要來到守護者面前
i.ev: Tibetan/academic: directly in the presence of the protector; 'all' (都) is unnatural and unsupported here, and 'must come' is odd.
i.fx: 我來到守護者面前，因為害怕痛苦而雙手合十。

atts.t: 我來到守護者面前，因為害怕痛苦而雙手合十。我一次又一次鞠躬敬禮，坦承這一切。
只要是不會傷害到他們自己的事，就隨便他們對我做吧。希望不管在什麼時候，都不會有任何一個人因為我而白忙一場。

i.sp: 不會有任何一個人因為我而白忙一場
i.ev: Academic: 'may no one who relates to me ever end up with something futile/meaningless' (anyone connected to me should benefit); 'wasted effort because of me' shifts the sense toward people's effort being wasted.
i.fx: 希望不管在什麼時候，只要有人看到我、想到我，都不會空手而回，都能得到好處。

atts.t: 只要是不會傷害到他們自己的事，就隨便他們對我做吧。希望不管在什麼時候，只要有人遇到我、想到我，都不會空手而回，都能得到好處。

i.sp: 就隨便他們對我做吧 / 只要有人遇到我、想到我
i.ev: Academic: "whatever action does not harm them, let them do it; in relation to me, may none be in vain". "Do to me" and "meet me, think of me / get benefit" are not stated.
i.fx: 只要是不會傷害到他們自己的事，就讓他們去做吧。希望不管在什麼時候，只要和我有關，就不會有人白費力氣。

atts.t: 從現在開始不管怎樣，我都要做符合這個家族的事。這是一個完美又尊貴的家族，我絕對不能弄髒它的名聲。

i.sp: 我絕對不能弄髒它的名聲
i.ev: Academic: "不令染污" this faultless noble lineage; no mention of reputation/name, only not defiling the lineage.
i.fx: 我絕對不能弄髒這個家族。

atts.t: 從現在開始不管怎樣，我都要做符合這個家族的事。這是一個完美又尊貴的家族，我絕對不能弄髒這個家族。
如果嚴重的墮落，和強大的覺悟之心，在輪迴中交替出現。我就要花很久的時間，才能達到覺悟的階段。

i.sp: 才能達到覺悟的階段
i.ev: Academic: 得地將歷時久遠 (attaining a bhumi/stage takes long); locked term for ས is 階段. "覺悟的階段" may be read as full enlightenment.
i.fx: 我就要花很久的時間，才能走到菩薩修行的更高階段。

atts.t: 如果嚴重的墮落，和強大的覺悟之心，在輪迴中交替出現。我就要花很久的時間，才能走到菩薩修行的更高階段。

i.sp: 如果嚴重的墮落，和強大的覺悟之心，在輪迴中交替出現。我就要花很久
i.ev: The "if" clause is cut off by a full stop from its main clause, which is ungrammatical.
i.fx: 如果嚴重的墮落，和強大的覺悟之心，在輪迴中交替出現，我就要花很久的時間，才能走到菩薩修行的更高階段。

atts.t: 如來來到世界上，讓我得到信任和人的身體，還能這麼適合做好事。這些事情都非常少見，什麼時候才能再得到呢？

i.sp: 如來來到世界上，讓我得到信任和人的身體
i.ev: Academic lists three separate rare conditions: a Tathagata appearing, gaining faith and a human body, and suitability for good deeds; the Tathagata is not said to give them to me.
i.fx: 如來出現在世界上、我有信任、又得到人的身體，還這麼適合做好事。這些事情都非常少見，什麼時候才能再得到呢？

atts.t: 如來出現在世界上、我有信任、又得到人的身體，還這麼適合做好事。這些事情都非常少見，什麼時候才能再得到呢？
如果我不做好事，卻累積很多有害的行為，就算過了好幾百個漫長歲月，我也連快樂的去處的聲音都聽不到。

i.sp: 就算過了好幾百個漫長歲月
i.ev: Academic: 縱然歷經百俱胝劫 (a hundred kotis of kalpas, about a billion); "several hundred" gravely understates the number.
i.fx: 如果我不做好事，卻累積很多有害的行為，就算過了數以億計的漫長歲月，我也連快樂的去處的聲音都聽不到。

atts.t: 如果我不做好事，卻累積很多有害的行為。就算過了數以億計的漫長歲月，我也連快樂的去處的聲音都聽不到。
這些輪迴監獄的守衛，也是在地獄等地方傷害我的兇手。如果它們住在我心裡緊抓不放的網中，我怎麼可能會快樂呢？

i.sp: 在地獄等地方傷害我的兇手
i.ev: Academic: 於地獄等作劊子者 (executioners in hell; Tibetan gsod byed gshed ma = killing executioner). 'Hurt me' and 'murderer' is imprecise: they are the ones who carry out the killing/punishing.
i.fx: 也是在地獄等地方行刑、折磨我們的劊子手。

atts.t: 這些輪迴監獄的守衛，也是在地獄等地方行刑、折磨我們的劊子手。如果它們住在我心裡緊抓不放的網中，我怎麼可能會快樂呢？
我要堅持這個決心，帶著敵意去戰鬥。雖然這也是一種心裡的煩惱，但因為它能摧毀心裡的煩惱，所以是個例外。

i.sp: 我要堅持這個決心，帶著敵意去戰鬥
i.ev: Academic: 我當貪著於此，懷著怨恨而交戰 (I will be attached to this and fight with resentment). The point is that the attachment and resentment are themselves afflictions, hence the 'exception'; 'hold on to this resolve' loses the attachment and makes it unclear which affliction is meant.
i.fx: 我要對打敗煩惱這件事緊緊抓著不放，帶著怨恨去跟它們作戰。這種抓著不放和怨恨，本來也是煩惱，但因為它能摧毀心裡的煩惱，所以是個例外。

atts.t: 我要對打敗煩惱這件事緊抓不放，帶著怨恨去跟它們作戰。這種緊抓不放和怨恨，本來也是心裡的煩惱，但因為它能摧毀心裡的煩惱，所以是個例外。
像是老虎、獅子、大象和熊，還有毒蛇和所有的敵人。甚至是「地獄的看守」、壞巫師，以及可怕的「食人妖怪」。

i.sp: 壞巫師
i.ev: Academic: 女巫 (Tibetan byad ma, a female witch/sorceress); 'bad' is added and the female sense is lost.
i.fx: 女巫

atts.t: 像是老虎、獅子、大象和熊，還有毒蛇和所有的敵人。甚至是地獄的看守、女巫，還有食人妖怪。
「眾生的地獄」裡有許多武器，那是誰特意做出來的？燒得滾燙的鐵地是誰造的？那些可怕的女子又是從哪裡來的？

i.sp: 那些可怕的女子
i.ev: Academic: 彼等女眾從何而生 (no 'frightening'). Note also that the Tibetan reads me tshogs (masses of fire), not women, so the academic translation and the Tibetan differ here; the children's text follows the academic but adds 'frightening'.
i.fx: 那些女子又是從哪裡來的？

atts.t: 眾生的地獄裡有許多武器，那是誰特意做出來的？燒得滾燙的鐵地是誰造的？那些女子又是從哪裡來的？
只要生起一個清楚明白的心，就會得到很好的結果，比如生在梵天。如果只有身體和言語在做，心卻沒有跟上，這行為就很微弱，得不到這樣的結果。

i.sp: 如果只有身體和言語在做，心卻沒有跟上
i.ev: Academic: even the result of an act accompanied by body and speech is not like that (of one clear mind), because the conduct is weak. It does not say the mind 'did not keep up'; the children's text adds that explanation, and also turns 'Brahma and so on' into a single example.
i.fx: 只要生起一個清楚明白的心，就會得到像生在梵天那樣的結果。但是，就算身體和言語一起去做，因為這樣的行為力量很弱，也得不到這樣的結果。

atts.t: 只要生起一個清楚明白的心，就會得到像生在梵天那樣的結果。但是，就算伴隨著身體和言語一起去做，因為這樣的行為力量很弱，也得不到這樣的結果。
我們可以跟著老師學習，聽從為我授戒的老師的教導。如果我們因為害怕做錯事而心生恭敬，仔細留意就能很輕鬆地生起。

i.sp: 因為害怕做錯事而心生恭敬
i.ev: Academic: the fortunate one who feels respect out of fear; the object of the fear is not specified. 'Fear of doing wrong' is added, and the 'fortunate/destined' (有緣者) qualifier is dropped.
i.fx: 如果有緣的人因為心裡有敬畏而生起恭敬，仔細留意就能很輕鬆地生起。

atts.t: 我們可以跟著老師學習，聽從為我授戒的老師的教導。如果有緣的人因為敬畏而心生恭敬，仔細留意就能很輕鬆地生起。

i.sp: 因為敬畏而心生恭敬
i.ev: Academic: respect arises "out of fear" (畏懼); "敬畏" (awe/reverence) shifts the sense.
i.fx: 如果有緣的人因為心裡害怕而生起恭敬，仔細留意就能很輕鬆地生起。

atts.t: 當我聽到各種無聊的話語，或是看到許多神奇的景象。如果我參與其中，就要捨棄，不要對它們緊抓不放。

i.sp: 如果我參與其中，就要捨棄，不要對它們緊抓不放
i.ev: Academic: when engaging in all these (idle talk, spectacles), one should abandon attachment to them. The children's 'then abandon' can be read as abandoning the activity itself.
i.fx: 如果我參與其中，也要放下對它們的緊抓不放。

atts.t: 當我聽到各種無聊的話語，或是看到許多新奇的景象。如果我參與其中，也要放下對它們的緊抓不放。

i.sp: 當我聽到各種無聊的話語，或是看到許多新奇的景象。如果我參與其中
i.ev: The "when" clause is split from its main clause by a full stop; "聽到/看到" then "參與其中" is redundant and ungrammatical.
i.fx: 當我參與各種無聊的話語，或是許多新奇的景象時，要放下對它們的緊抓不放。

atts.t: 面對那些沒有可責備的事情，即使是為了自己和眾生去做，也要把它們看成像變出來的東西一樣，沒有真正的「我」。我應該永遠保持這樣的心思。

i.sp: 即使是為了自己和眾生去做，也要把它們看成像變出來的東西一樣
i.ev: Academic: 'under the control of oneself and sentient beings, like a conjured appearance without I, one should always hold this mind.' The children's text turns 'subject to self and beings' into 'doing it for the sake of' them, and makes the conjured-thing simile describe the deeds rather than how the mind is held.
i.fx: 面對那些沒有可責備的事情，我和眾生都能做主。我的心思要像變出來的東西一樣，不緊抓著「我」。我應該永遠保持這樣的心思。

atts.t: 面對那些沒有可責備的事情，我和眾生都能做主。我的心思要像變出來的東西一樣，不緊抓著「我」。我應該永遠保持這樣的心思。
替別人高興這件事，這輩子對我沒有任何損失，下輩子也會帶來巨大的快樂。相反地，因為過錯而產生不開心和痛苦，下輩子更會帶來巨大的痛苦。

i.sp: 替別人高興這件事
i.ev: Academic: 'in this life there is no loss for me, in the next a great happiness'; it does not name the subject (the verse's referent is left implicit). The children's text supplies 'rejoicing in others' as the cause.
i.fx: 這樣做，這輩子對我沒有任何損失，下輩子也會帶來巨大的快樂。相反地，因為過錯而產生不開心和痛苦，下輩子更會帶來巨大的痛苦。

atts.t: 這樣做，這輩子對我沒有任何損失，下輩子也會帶來巨大的快樂。相反地，因為過錯而產生不開心和痛苦，下輩子更會帶來巨大的痛苦。

i.sp: 下輩子更會帶來巨大的痛苦
i.ev: Academic: "in the next life there is also great suffering" (亦有大苦); "更" (even more) adds a comparison that is not there.
i.fx: 下輩子也會帶來巨大的痛苦。

atts.t: 帶著堅定的心意去幫忙，或是用解藥去對付壞習慣。只要對象是有著美好的品質的人、對我們有恩的人，或是正在承受痛苦的人，這都會變成很大的好事。

i.sp: 帶著堅定的心意去幫忙，或是用解藥去對付壞習慣
i.ev: Academic: the action is 'prompted by constant strong inclination, or prompted by an antidote'; it then becomes great virtue toward qualities, benefactors and the suffering. The children's text narrows the action to 'helping' and the antidote to 'dealing with bad habits', neither of which is in the text.
i.fx: 如果是帶著強烈的心意去做，或是靠解藥的力量去做，而對象是有美好品質的人、對我們有恩的人，或是正在受苦的人，這就會成為很大的好事。

atts.t: 如果是帶著強烈的心意去做，或是靠解藥的力量去做。只要對象是有美好的品質的人、對我們有恩的人，或是正在承受痛苦的人，這就會成為很大的好事。

i.ev: Academic says the action is prompted "always" (恆) by strong intention; the children's text drops "always".
i.fx: 如果是一直帶著強烈的心意去做，或是靠解藥的力量去做。

atts.t: 遇到受苦的人、無依無靠的人，還有正在做嚴格的修行的人，我們都要分東西給他們。自己只要吃剛好的量就好，除了僧人的三種衣袍以外，其他東西都可以送給別人。

i.sp: 遇到受苦的人
i.ev: Academic: 墮惡趣者 (those fallen into bad states/wrong ways), not simply 'people who suffer'; also 'should give away all except the three robes' is softened to 'can be given'.
i.fx: 遇到墮入惡道的人、無依無靠的人，還有正在做嚴格修行的人，我們要分東西給他們。自己只吃剛好的量，除了僧人的三種衣袍以外，其他東西都要送給別人。

atts.t: 遇到墮入惡道的人、無依無靠的人，還有正在做嚴格的修行的人，我們要分東西給他們。自己只吃剛好的量，除了僧人的三種衣袍以外，其他東西都要送給別人。
對於心胸狹窄的人，我不說深奧廣大的佛法。如果沒有男生在場，我也不單獨對女生說。不管是基礎還是高深的佛法，我都應該用同樣恭敬的心去實踐。

i.sp: 心胸狹窄的人
